question: Property insurance claims automation team runs a GenAI assistant on Bedrock (Converse/InvokeModelWithResponseStream). Client-side invocation errors are rising and responses are sometimes malformed. Payloads can exceed 100KB. They need to inspect model inputs/outputs, correlate by claim/experiment ID, keep logs in the workload account/Region, and avoid a proxy in the inference path. What should they do?
options: A) Enable CloudTrail with advanced event selectors; query by model/identity/claim/experiment
B) Enable Bedrock model invocation logging per Region with an S3 destination in the same account/Region; pass caller metadata for claim/experiment IDs
C) Enable Bedrock model invocation logging per Region with a CloudWatch Logs destination in the same account/Region; pass caller metadata
D) Enable Bedrock model invocation logging centrally with a CloudWatch Logs destination in a security account; pass caller metadata
explanation: Model invocation logging (not CloudTrail) captures actual prompt/response payloads for supported bedrock-runtime ops. Destination must be same account+Region as source. CloudWatch Logs caps captured JSON at 100KB, so S3 is required when payloads can exceed that. CloudTrail only gives API audit (who/when), not payload content.
group: Bedrock Model Invocation Logging vs CloudTrail
comparison_note: Distinguishes CloudTrail (audit only, never payload) from Bedrock invocation logging (payload capture), and within invocation logging, S3 vs CloudWatch Logs turns on the 100KB payload-size ceiling. Same-account/same-Region is a hard constraint — a centralized security-account destination is invalid regardless of log-store choice.

question: A university registrar's Bedrock advising assistant needs centrally managed instructions, JSON response rules, runtime variables ({{term}}, {{program}}), an immutable production config, and both-side guardrail safeguards. The static instruction portion must be eligible for Prompt management prompt caching, and apps already use Converse. Which implementation needs the LEAST application-side prompt logic?
options: A) CHAT prompt with variables, create a version, invoke Converse using the versioned prompt ARN as modelId, pass promptVariables, attach guardrailConfig
B) CHAT prompt with variables, create a version, invoke Converse with the base model ID, render the template into messages/system, attach guardrailConfig
C) TEXT prompt with variables, create a version, invoke via versioned ARN, pass promptVariables, enable prompt caching, attach guardrailConfig
D) CHAT prompt with variables, save/test the DRAFT, invoke via DRAFT prompt ARN, pass promptVariables, attach guardrailConfig
explanation: A managed prompt invoked through Converse uses the versioned prompt ARN as modelId; the app should not re-send messages/system since those live in the template. CHAT (not TEXT) template type is required for Prompt management prompt caching. A version, not a mutable draft, is required for an immutable production artifact.
group: Bedrock Prompt Management: CHAT vs TEXT, Draft vs Version
comparison_note: Group anchor for the CHAT-vs-TEXT-caching trap (repeats in 007, 026): TEXT prompts support variables/versions/guardrails fine, but only CHAT is eligible for prompt caching. Also tests draft-vs-version: draft is mutable, unsuitable for 'immutable production config.'

question: A pharmacy team maintains five Prompt management candidate prompt configurations and must run a fixed regression suite before promotion. The process must preserve approved prompt text + inference config for rollback, support automation (not visual review), and publish pass/fail to CloudWatch. Best approach?
options: A) Evaluate the 3 highest-priority candidates with Prompt builder comparison, run Lambda checks on the selected draft, version that draft, publish to CloudWatch
B) Create prompt versions for release candidates, run a Step Functions regression workflow invoking prompts via Converse, validate with Lambda, emit outcomes to CloudWatch
C) Update the draft for each candidate, run a Lambda regression script via InvokeModelWithResponseStream for all supported text models, overwrite the draft after tests pass
D) Create separate Prompt management prompts per candidate, run a scheduled Lambda job, write pass/fail to CloudWatch Logs, copy the winning text into the production prompt
explanation: Prompt versions are point-in-time snapshots suitable for promotion/rollback; the console comparison UI supports only up to 3 variants, so it can't cover a 5-candidate gate. Step Functions + Lambda + CloudWatch is the automated regression-gate pattern. Prompt management prompts work with InvokeModel/InvokeModelWithResponseStream only for Claude/Llama configs — not 'all supported text models' — so Converse is the safer invocation choice here.
group: Bedrock Prompt Management: CHAT vs TEXT, Draft vs Version
comparison_note: Same family as 002/026 but the trap here is scale (5 candidates vs 3-variant console comparison limit) and snapshot semantics (version vs draft vs 'copy winning text') rather than the CHAT/TEXT caching distinction.

question: A legal-aid intake team's single-paragraph Bedrock prompt produces inconsistent classification: extra prose, missing metadata fields, drifting labels after minor edits. They want low-overhead consistency, prompt-change comparison, reuse of an approved prompt in the app, and validation beyond just the tuning examples. Best approach?
options: A) Reusable prompt with variables/variants in Bedrock; add clear sections, separators, and an output indicator; test variants on a dev set; version the best prompt; verify with a hold-out set
B) Prompt variants adding step-by-step reasoning + requested JSON format; compare in Prompt Management; version the preferred prompt; use in inference
C) Run OptimizePrompt for the existing prompt/model; add examples; manually compare original vs optimized; store chosen prompt in app config
D) Enable model invocation logging; review CloudWatch logs; sample outputs for human review; update prompt text in source control; deploy
explanation: Bedrock prompt-design guidance recommends clear sections/separators/output indicators for classification tasks, plus a dev set during iteration and a hold-out set to verify the final prompt (avoiding overfitting to tuning examples). Prompt Management provides the versioned reuse layer. OptimizePrompt is a fast single-model heuristic rewrite, not a full lifecycle+hold-out workflow; logging alone isn't a quality gate.
group: Bedrock Prompt Management: CHAT vs TEXT, Draft vs Version
comparison_note: Rounds out the Prompt Management trio: 002 tests CHAT/TEXT caching eligibility, 007 tests candidate-scale regression gating, this one tests prompt-structuring technique + dev-set/hold-out-set discipline as the differentiator from partial answers (B lacks structural rework + hold-out; C lacks versioning/hold-out; D lacks structured lifecycle).

question: A regional airline's incident-triage app requires operations-manager review (up to 10 days) before high-risk remediation runs. Managers submit decisions via an internal HTTPS endpoint; the workflow must not keep compute idle. Best orchestration?
options: A) Step Functions Standard Workflow, Lambda callback task w/ .waitForTaskToken; send the task token to a shared tooling account; API Gateway invokes Lambda there to call SendTaskSuccess/Failure
B) Step Functions Standard Workflow with a Wait state; review endpoint writes decision to DynamoDB; workflow periodically polls via Lambda

C) Step Functions Standard Workflow, Lambda callback task w/ .waitForTaskToken; pass $$.Task.Token to the review endpoint; API Gateway invokes Lambda to call SendTaskSuccess/Failure in the WORKFLOW account
D) Step Functions EXPRESS Workflow, Lambda callback task w/ .waitForTaskToken; pass $$.Task.Token to the review endpoint; API Gateway invokes Lambda in the workflow account
explanation: Standard Workflows support long-running durable executions (Express is capped, unsuitable for a 10-day wait). The task-token callback pattern avoids idle compute; SendTaskSuccess/Failure MUST be called by a principal in the SAME account as the workflow — a shared tooling account cannot complete the callback directly.
comparison_note: Paired with 017: this question isolates the SAME-ACCOUNT task-token constraint and Standard-vs-Express duration limit. 017 reuses the correct pattern but adds Parallel+Choice states and a bounded-revision-loop context on top of the same callback mechanism.

question: A pharma regulatory team's workflow: normalize intake JSON, run two Bedrock prompt-checks in parallel, merge findings, revise up to 3x on failure, then wait for a reviewer (up to 7 days) to approve/reject. They need deterministic transitions, durable state, and full audit history with minimal custom state code. Best implementation?
options: A) Step Functions Standard workflow: Lambda+Bedrock integrations, Parallel and Choice states, bounded revision paths, task-token callback for reviewer approval
B) Strands Agents app with AWS Agent Squad routing; persist state in DynamoDB; call Bedrock and reviewer APIs from worker agents
C) Bedrock agent with action groups for checking/revision/approval; enable tracing; let the agent choose the next tool from context
D) Bedrock Flow with prompt/condition/Lambda nodes; implement the bounded revision counter in Lambda; invoke the flow per request
explanation: Standard Workflows natively provide Parallel states, Choice-based branching, retry/catch for the bounded revision loop, and the task-token callback for a multi-day human handoff — all with built-in execution history. Agents/Strands add unneeded planning autonomy and custom state management for what is a fixed, deterministic process; Bedrock Flows lack the same depth of durable orchestration controls for a multi-day external callback.
comparison_note: Paired with 003: 003 isolates the same-account task-token rule against a shared-tooling-account distractor; this question is the 'full recipe' version combining Parallel + Choice + bounded retries + callback, contrasted against agent/Flow/DynamoDB-state alternatives that lack Step Functions' native durable orchestration.

question: A maritime logistics Bedrock RAG assistant faces jailbreak prompts in chat and prompt-injection hidden in uploaded manifests. The team needs managed runtime detection where possible plus repeatable adversarial tests before each release, without training/hosting a custom safety model. (Select TWO.)
options: A) Automated adversarial test workflow replaying jailbreak prompts and poisoned-document samples through ApplyGuardrail and the app path before release
B) Analyze CloudTrail records after release; block IAM principals with suspicious invocation patterns
C) Run Macie discovery jobs on the manifest bucket; quarantine files with sensitive-data findings
D) Configure Bedrock Guardrails with prompt attack, denied topic, and harmful content filters; apply to chat requests and model responses
E) Configure AWS WAF managed rule groups on API Gateway; tune SQLi/XSS rules to inspect bodies for jailbreak text
explanation: Guardrails' prompt-attack/content filters are the managed runtime control. ApplyGuardrail lets the team test retrieved/injected content independent of a model call, enabling a repeatable pre-release adversarial regression suite. CloudTrail is audit-only, Macie is a DLP/PII discovery tool (not injection-intent detection), and WAF targets HTTP-layer attacks, not semantic jailbreak text.
comparison_note: Pairs with 034 on ApplyGuardrail usage: this question is about WHICH controls to combine (Guardrails filters + a replay-based test harness) vs 034 which is about WHERE in a Step Functions Map workflow to place ApplyGuardrail calls and IAM enforcement.

question: A Standard Step Functions state machine uses a Map state per taxpayer letter: guardrail precheck, FM call via Lambda (up to 90s), guardrail postcheck, then write accepted draft or review record. A stalled FM call must only send THAT letter to review; other Map items continue. Security also requires blocking Bedrock calls that omit the approved guardrail. Best implementation?
options: A) ApplyGuardrail INPUT+OUTPUT inside each Map item; invoke Bedrock via a Step Functions HTTP Task with TimeoutSeconds set above 90s; catch per-item timeout; explicit Deny on bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier
B) ApplyGuardrail INPUT+OUTPUT inside each Map item; invoke Bedrock via Lambda with configured timeouts; catch timeout failures on the MAP STATE; explicit Deny on bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier

C) ApplyGuardrail INPUT+OUTPUT inside each Map item; invoke Bedrock via Lambda with configured timeouts; catch PER-ITEM timeout failures INSIDE the Map item; explicit Deny on bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier

D) ApplyGuardrail INPUT+OUTPUT inside each Map item; invoke Bedrock via Lambda with configured timeouts; catch per-item timeout failures; use Guardrails CloudWatch metrics to enforce approved guardrail usage
explanation: Step Functions HTTP Task has a hard 60s max duration regardless of configured TimeoutSeconds, ruling out A for 90s calls. Catch must be placed INSIDE each Map item (not on the Map state as a whole) to isolate only the stalled letter. CloudWatch metrics are observability, not an authorization control — only an IAM explicit Deny on bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier can block non-compliant inference calls.
comparison_note: Companion to 004: same ApplyGuardrail(INPUT/OUTPUT) mechanic, but the trap here is workflow plumbing (HTTP Task 60s ceiling, catch scope inside vs outside Map item) and IAM enforcement vs CloudWatch-metrics-as-a-control.

question: A CI/CD regression gate must run an unattended Bedrock model evaluation against 900 summarization prompts with reference summaries in S3 (.jsonl). Many teams run eval jobs daily. The gate must preserve auditable results, not treat job submission as completion, and fail if the model doesn't produce responses for the full benchmark. Best approach?
options: A) Automatic ModelEvaluation job from S3 .jsonl, roleArn + outputDataConfig.s3Uri, poll ListEvaluationJobs w/ nextToken until terminal, fail on total prompt count or aggregate metric regressions
B) Automatic ModelEvaluation job from S3 .jsonl, roleArn + outputDataConfig.s3Uri, poll ListEvaluationJobs w/ nextToken until terminal, fail on MISSING RESPONSES or metric regressions
C) Automatic ModelEvaluation job with TWO inference profiles (baseline + candidate), poll until terminal, fail on comparison regressions
D) Automatic RagEvaluation job from the S3 .jsonl dataset, roleArn + outputDataConfig.s3Uri, poll until terminal, fail on missing responses or metric regressions
explanation: CreateEvaluationJob returns 202/jobArn asynchronously — job creation is not completion; the pipeline must poll to a terminal status. Automatic model evaluation jobs support only ONE model/inference profile (two-model comparison needs human-worker evaluation). RagEvaluation is the wrong job type for a plain summarization benchmark. Critically, total prompt COUNT can mask that some prompts never got a response — only prompts WITH responses feed metric calculations, so the gate must check response coverage, not just aggregate scores.
group: Bedrock Evaluation Jobs: Async Completion & Response Coverage
comparison_note: Anchors the eval-jobs group with 029: same 'total prompts vs responses received' trap and same async-completion trap, but 029 adds task-type partitioning (1600 prompts, 2 task types, 1000-prompt-per-job limit) on top.

question: An unattended regression gate must measure built-in automatic evaluation metrics for BOTH summarization and classification from a 1,600-prompt benchmark (S3, with optional category tags), preserve auditable results, and not pass a release when the model fails to return responses for part of the benchmark. (Select TWO.)
options: A) Track evaluation job completion with status-aware pagination, read the S3 .jsonl result files, fail on score regression OR insufficient response coverage
B) Enable model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs + S3; calculate regression pass/fail from logged prompts, responses, and token metrics
C) Run one human-worker ModelEvaluation job with baseline+candidate models; approve when CreateEvaluationJob returns HTTP 202 jobArn
D) Call CreateEvaluationJob for SEPARATE automatic ModelEvaluation jobs BY TASK TYPE, S3 JSON Lines dataset (.jsonl), no more than 1,000 prompts per job
E) Submit ONE automatic ModelEvaluation job covering both task types and all 1,600 prompts; use category-level scores to approve/reject
explanation: Automatic evaluation jobs support one task type per job and up to 1,000 prompts per job — 1,600 prompts across 2 task types must be split into multiple jobs. A 202/jobArn response only means the job was accepted, never completed; the gate must poll to terminal status and check response coverage before trusting aggregate scores.
group: Bedrock Evaluation Jobs: Async Completion & Response Coverage
comparison_note: Same coverage-and-completion trap as 013, plus the 1,000-prompt/1-task-type-per-job partitioning rule that 013 didn't need (900 prompts, 1 task type fit in a single job).

question: An insurance claims Bedrock assistant needs a CI/CD release gate covering 1,600 prompts (single-turn lookups + six-turn conversations) that separately assesses retrieved context quality, generated answer quality, safety, AND subjective usefulness (weekly specialist review), minimizing custom evaluation code. (Select TWO.)
options: A) Run one retrieve-only RAG evaluation against the Knowledge Base; use Correctness, Faithfulness, Harmfulness, and Refusal to assess contexts and final answers
B) Configure EvaluationDatasetMetricConfig with CitationPrecision and CitationCoverage for retrieve-and-generate jobs; use those as release-blocking controls
C) Partition prompt data into S3 JSON Lines files of 1,000 prompts or fewer; single-turn records for retrieval tests, conversations capped at FIVE turns for generation tests
D) Run Bedrock RAG evaluation jobs for retrieval AND retrieve-and-generate assessment, PLUS LLM-as-a-judge and human-worker evaluations for sampled generated responses
E) Submit the complete prompt history as one S3 JSONL file to a retrieve-and-generate job; use the job output as the ONLY release gate
explanation: Retrieve-only jobs evaluate CONTEXT (ContextRelevance/ContextCoverage), not generated answers — so option A's metric list is wrong for that job type. CitationPrecision/CitationCoverage aren't valid EvaluationDatasetMetricConfig names. RAG prompt datasets: single-turn for retrieve-only, up to 5 turns for retrieve-and-generate — a six-turn conversation exceeds that limit and must be handled accordingly. Combining RAG evaluation + LLM-as-a-judge + human-worker evaluation covers context, answer quality/safety, and subjective usefulness without custom code.
group: Bedrock Evaluation Jobs: Async Completion & Response Coverage
comparison_note: Rounds out the evaluation-jobs trio: 013/029 focus on ModelEvaluation job mechanics (completion, coverage, task-type limits); this one shifts to RAG-specific evaluation job types, valid metric names, and conversation-turn limits.

question: A Bedrock custom knowledge base uses OpenSearch Serverless with the nmslib engine; embeddings are stored but raw text isn't a filterable field. Queries mix exact policy codes with natural language. Need better relevance/speed without an extra model call in the request path. Best approach?
options: A) Keep nmslib, add equals filters; call Retrieve with vectorSearchConfiguration filters and HYBRID search
B) Keep the current index; configure implicitFilterConfiguration with a Claude model; call Retrieve with SEMANTIC search and generated metadata filters
C) Move to a fully managed KB with managedSearchConfiguration; call Retrieve with semantic search and a larger numberOfResults
D) Rebuild the OpenSearch Serverless index with the FAISS engine and a filterable text field; call Retrieve with vectorSearchConfiguration metadata filters and HYBRID search
explanation: Bedrock Knowledge Bases require the FAISS engine (not nmslib) for metadata filtering on OpenSearch Serverless vector indexes; hybrid search additionally needs a filterable text field. Implicit filtering adds a model-based preprocessing call, violating the no-extra-model-call constraint. Managed KBs always use hybrid via managedSearchConfiguration and don't offer semantic-only.
comparison_note: Group anchor: 019 and 024 repeat the same faiss-not-nmslib rule in different contexts (vector-store selection vs deployment-gate validation).

question: A private-equity RAG assistant needs semantic retrieval for narrative text plus exact-match influence for ticker symbols/clause IDs/product codes where the vector store supports it. Security allows the approved OpenSearch Service managed clusters or another documented Bedrock KB vector-store integration; must use Bedrock KB retrieval/citations, not a custom retriever. (Select TWO.)
options: A) Knowledge Base backed by S3 Vectors using BINARY embeddings, large parent-chunk metadata, metadata keys for every source attribute
B) Customer-managed Knowledge Base backed by OpenSearch vector indexes; configure supported vector search, matching dimensions, raw-text fields, and Bedrock metadata fields
C) Bedrock retrieval HYBRID only for supported RDS/OpenSearch Serverless/MongoDB vector stores with a filterable text field; use SEMANTIC otherwise
D) OpenSearch managed-cluster indexes with the NMSLIB engine, matching embedding dimensions, raw-text fields, and Bedrock metadata fields
E) Bedrock retrieval HYBRID for EVERY vector store; request more than 100 results to compensate for parent replacement
explanation: A customer-managed OpenSearch KB is a valid documented vector-store path with the right field mappings. Hybrid search is conditional — only documented for RDS, OpenSearch Serverless, and MongoDB with a filterable text field; OpenSearch Service managed clusters are valid but not documented for hybrid, so semantic is the fallback. S3 Vectors uses float embeddings (not binary); nmslib is unsupported for the search vector on OpenSearch managed clusters; numberOfResults has a documented max under 100.
comparison_note: Same faiss/nmslib and vector-store-support family as 012/024, but the twist here is that hybrid-search eligibility (not filtering eligibility) depends on store type — OpenSearch managed clusters support Bedrock KB retrieval but not documented hybrid search.

question: A customer-provisioned OpenSearch Serverless vector index (via IaC) backs a Bedrock KB. Recent releases caused retrieval degradation from index drift, and a large ingestion job spiked storage. Need a deployment gate validating the index, CloudWatch alarms for runtime failures/throttling, and storage reported only once ingestion data is reliably measurable. Best approach?
options: A) Gate verifies a FAISS vector field with matching dims, records collectionARN/vectorIndexName/vectorField/textField/metadataField; alarms on Invocations/ClientErrors/ServerErrors/Throttles and IN-PROGRESS RawDataSize
B) Gate verifies a FAISS vector field with matching dims, records the same fields; alarms on the same metrics plus POST-INGESTION RawDataSize
C) Gate verifies an NMSLIB vector field with matching dims, records the same fields; alarms including post-ingestion RawDataSize
D) Gate verifies a FAISS vector field with matching dims, records collectionARN/vectorIndexName/vectorField/textField and an EXTERNAL METADATA TABLE; alarms including post-ingestion RawDataSize
explanation: Bedrock KB setup for OpenSearch Serverless requires FAISS and a Bedrock-managed metadataField (not an external table). RawDataSize is published only AFTER an ingestion job completes, so it's a post-ingestion signal, not usable for in-progress monitoring. Throttles (429) are tracked separately from ClientErrors/ServerErrors.
comparison_note: Third of the faiss-engine trio (with 012, 019); this one adds the RawDataSize timing trap (post- vs in-progress) and the metadataField-must-be-Bedrock-managed detail.

question: A customs-procedures Bedrock KB assistant needs a pre-display accuracy verifier that inspects source chunks/metadata, uses a per-chunk relevance signal, and rejects answers not matching a required JSON structure — without treating the KB as an intrinsic truth-checker. Best approach?
options: A) Call Retrieve with numberOfResults=100, accept any answer with matching metadata, treat high relevance scores as factual confidence
B) Call RetrieveAndGenerate, require citations, compare each claim to retrievedReferences content/metadata
C) Call RetrieveAndGenerate, require citations for every sentence, use retrievedReferences content as the required JSON contract
D) Call Retrieve, validate model output against a JSON Schema, compare each claim to the returned content/metadata/documentId/relevance score
explanation: Retrieve exposes raw evidence (content, documentId, metadata, relevance score) that application logic can independently verify with JSON Schema validation — relevance is not factuality, so a high score alone can't confirm a claim is true. RetrieveAndGenerate's citation structure lacks a per-result relevance score and doesn't double as a JSON contract.
comparison_note: Anchors the Retrieve-vs-RetrieveAndGenerate trio with 020 (tool-abstraction design) and 025 (citation-based audit trail) — same API distinction, different downstream purpose (verification vs multi-assistant tool design vs auditability).

question: Multiple internal assistants share one RAG retrieval layer over Bedrock KBs (via tool/function interfaces) but each chooses its own FM, prompt template, formatting, and citation handling AFTER retrieval. The vector store may change over time, so avoid non-portable search settings. Least integration risk?
options: A) Application-owned search tool with a JSON parameter schema; execute in client code by calling Retrieve, then pass chunks to the selected FM
B) Application-owned answer tool with a JSON parameter schema; execute by calling RetrieveAndGenerate, then return the generated answer to callers
C) Agent action group for vector search with both an OpenAPI schema and a function schema; model invokes the KB operation directly
D) Reusable retrieval tool that always sets overrideSearchType to HYBRID; execute against every knowledge base
explanation: Retrieve returns evidence only, letting each assistant own generation/formatting/citations independently — RetrieveAndGenerate would centralize generation in the shared layer, coupling all assistants to one model/prompt/citation style. Action groups use EITHER an OpenAPI schema OR a function schema, never both. Forcing HYBRID everywhere isn't portable — HYBRID requires specific vector-store support.
comparison_note: Same Retrieve-vs-RetrieveAndGenerate core as 006, applied to multi-tenant tool design; also reuses the HYBRID-portability trap from the faiss group (012/019/024).

question: An insurance claims team drafts settlement summaries via Bedrock KBs. Investigators can see the final summary and model ID but can't reliably trace which retrieved chunks supported each passage. They want deterministic audit without a custom citation parser (Glue Data Catalog already tracks source locations/schemas). Best implementation?
options: A) Capture Citation objects from RetrieveAndGenerate; persist generatedResponsePart and retrievedReferences with each answer; retain Glue Data Catalog identifiers
B) Prompt the model to print citation footnotes; persist the rendered footnote text; retain Glue Data Catalog identifiers
C) Store source identifiers in Glue table properties; parse matching identifiers from each answer; retain the parsed values
D) Call Retrieve before generation; persist the returned chunks with each answer; retain Glue Data Catalog identifiers
explanation: RetrieveAndGenerate's structured Citation objects (generatedResponsePart + retrievedReferences) give a deterministic generated-passage-to-source mapping — prompted footnotes are unreliable free text, and Glue Catalog is a metadata repository, not a citation/lineage mechanism. Retrieve alone (without generation) doesn't produce the passage-to-reference mapping needed here.
comparison_note: Completes the trio: unlike 006 (Retrieve for independent verification) and 020 (Retrieve for decoupled tool design), THIS scenario specifically wants RetrieveAndGenerate because it needs the built-in generated-passage-to-citation structure, not raw evidence.

question: Monthly aircraft inspection packages include scanned forms, PDFs, photos, videos, and voice notes. Need a normalized compliance record, transcripts/visual summaries, validation against a parts API, quarantine of failed packages, and a ServiceNow record only after validation — minimizing custom ML extraction code with retryable execution history. (Select TWO.)
options: A) Step Functions workflow invoking Textract, Transcribe, Comprehend, and Rekognition; merge outputs with Lambda; update ServiceNow
B) Bedrock Knowledge Base over the package files; query required fields with Lambda prompts; write cited answers + ticket updates to ServiceNow
C) Step Functions Standard workflow: EventBridge starts from each manifest, invokes extraction, validates with Lambda, quarantines failures, updates ServiceNow
D) Lambda integration reading extracted package metadata from S3, validating with the parts API, creating ServiceNow records, storing results
E) Configure Bedrock Data Automation with blueprints for the inspection schema; write JSON plus generated media artifacts to S3
explanation: Bedrock Data Automation with blueprints handles managed multimodal extraction (documents, images, video, audio) into a defined schema, minimizing custom extraction code. Step Functions Standard (EventBridge-triggered, with quarantine and post-validation ServiceNow update) supplies the durable orchestration. Chaining raw AI services (Textract/Transcribe/Comprehend/Rekognition) or a Knowledge Base requires far more custom merge/reconciliation logic; Lambda-only lacks durable branching/quarantine.
group: Multimodal Extraction via Bedrock Data Automation
comparison_note: Pairs with 033: same 'use BDA instead of stitching individual AI services' principle, applied to a museum archive scenario with an added PII-redaction requirement for oral-history audio.

question: A digital library's ingestion workflow covers scanned PDFs with tables, labeled photos, English oral-history audio with patient names, and CSV finding aids. Needs reviewable intermediate S3 artifacts, structure preservation, PII REDACTION from audio transcripts before indexing, and no custom/hosted extraction models. Lowest-overhead workflow?
options: A) Step Functions + SageMaker Processing custom containers for OCR, captioning, transcription, and CSV conversion; store JSON/Markdown outputs
B) Step Functions + Textract (PDFs/photos) + Transcribe with custom vocabulary (audio) + Comprehend to FLAG transcript PII for review + SageMaker Processing for CSV
C) Step Functions + Bedrock Data Automation blueprints (PDFs/photos) + Transcribe with custom vocabulary AND PII REDACTION (audio) + SageMaker Processing for CSV
D) Step Functions + a Bedrock multimodal model prompted for JSON/Markdown across PDFs, photos, audio, and CSV rows; store only the model responses
explanation: Bedrock Data Automation is the managed structured-extraction service for documents/images; Transcribe's PII redaction feature (not Comprehend's flag-only detection) is required to redact — not just flag — identifiers before indexing. Custom SageMaker containers and a single general-purpose prompted FM both trade away managed, modality-specific controls for more custom code and weaker schema consistency.
group: Multimodal Extraction via Bedrock Data Automation
comparison_note: Same BDA-over-custom-pipeline principle as 008; the added wrinkle here is choosing Transcribe's redaction (not Comprehend's flagging) to satisfy a hard 'redact before indexing' requirement.

question: Plant telemetry/notes/equipment IDs must be irreversibly tokenized on-prem before any request leaves the plant network; only the incident summary goes to Bedrock in a designated Region over private connectivity (no public endpoints), using managed AWS patterns without maintaining proxy fleets. (Select TWO.)
options: A) Create interface VPC endpoints for the required Bedrock runtime APIs in the designated Region; route plant traffic to those endpoints over the private connection
B) Deploy the normalization workflow in AWS Wavelength Zones near each site; send approved summaries to Bedrock through regional interface endpoints
C) Run plant workflows on AWS Outposts; connect each site to Bedrock via Direct Connect PUBLIC virtual interfaces for AWS service prefixes
D) Run the ingestion/normalization/tokenization workflow on AWS Outposts in each plant; transmit only approved incident summaries to the regional VPC
E) Run plant workflows on AWS Outposts; create interface VPC endpoints ONLY for the Bedrock CONTROL PLANE APIs
explanation: Two separate objectives: Outposts keeps local processing (tokenization) on-prem before anything leaves the plant, while Bedrock runtime interface VPC endpoints (PrivateLink) provide private IP access for the resulting summary. Direct Connect PUBLIC VIFs don't provide the PrivateLink path; a control-plane-only endpoint misses the runtime invocation API needed for inference; Wavelength doesn't move preprocessing into the plant network itself.
comparison_note: Pairs with 028 on the private-access theme: 021 is about physically keeping data on-prem (Outposts) plus reaching Bedrock privately (PrivateLink); 028 is about a downstream internal web app reaching Bedrock synchronously through a VPC-only API Gateway front door.

question: An internal EC2 web app (private subnets) needs a synchronous 'generate handoff brief' button combining user JSON, an internal HTTPS microservice call, and a Bedrock FM response. Endpoint must be VPC-only, no client-exposed AWS credentials, malformed JSON rejected before compute where possible, and throttled request rates. Least custom code?
options: A) API Gateway HTTP API with a VPC LINK; JWT authorizer; route throttling; Lambda integration calling the metadata service and Bedrock Runtime
B) API Gateway PRIVATE REST API via interface VPC endpoint; resource policy; request validation; throttling; DIRECT AWS SERVICE integration to Bedrock Runtime
C) API Gateway REGIONAL REST API with a Cognito authorizer; request validator; throttling; Lambda PROXY integration
D) API Gateway PRIVATE REST API via interface VPC endpoint; resource policy; request validation; throttling; Lambda PROXY integration calling the metadata service and Bedrock Runtime
explanation: A private REST API (reachable only via interface VPC endpoint, with a resource policy) is the VPC-only pattern — an HTTP API's VPC link connects OUTBOUND to private targets, it doesn't make the API itself VPC-only, and a regional REST API is public by default. A direct Bedrock service integration can't first call the internal metadata microservice — only Lambda proxy provides that orchestration step while still getting API Gateway's built-in validation/throttling for free.
comparison_note: Companion to 021: same PrivateLink/private-access family, but focused on inbound API-Gateway-to-caller privacy plus request orchestration, rather than outbound on-prem-to-Bedrock connectivity.

question: An agricultural dealer-technician Bedrock assistant handles high-volume lookups, warranty summaries, and low-volume complex troubleshooting. All traffic currently uses the most capable FM. Need lower spend while keeping troubleshooting quality at the current threshold, an evidence-based rollout plan, no fine-tuning, no hosting outside Bedrock. Most effective approach?
options: A) Prompt-length classifier via CountTokens; shorter requests to a smaller FM, longer to a larger FM; monitor aggregate token spend; tune thresholds from cost trends
B) Task-stratified prompt dataset; run Bedrock model evaluations for candidate FMs; choose the model with best average price-performance; route ALL request classes to that one model
C) Separate prompt templates per class; reduce response token limits for routine requests; keep the current FM for all traffic; buy provisioned throughput for peak periods

D) Task-stratified prompt dataset; run Bedrock model evaluations for candidate FMs; combine quality scores with token-based cost estimates; route EACH request class to the lowest-cost model meeting its quality threshold
explanation: Per-class evaluation (not a single aggregate winner or a prompt-length heuristic) prevents a good average score from hiding regressions in the high-risk troubleshooting class, while still letting routine/high-volume classes use cheaper models. Prompt length is not a reliable proxy for reasoning difficulty; keeping one model for all traffic limits savings.
comparison_note: Groups with 018 (CountTokens for request-time budget pruning) and 032 (max_tokens reservation vs EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage) — three different token/cost levers: model ROUTING (011), input CONTEXT PRUNING (018), and output CAP sizing (032).

question: A multilingual concierge assembles system prompt + recent turns + candidate RAG passages, then routes to one of several FMs, keeping the assembled input within a per-request token budget. Must avoid speculative model calls, preserve the most relevant passages when pruning, and cap response length. Most effective approach?
options: A) Invoke a smaller FM to summarize the assembled request; use its input count as the budget check; set an output token limit
B) Run a shared tokenizer before model routing; prune the assembled request to the shared count; set an output token limit
C) Estimate tokens from the prompt template at deployment time; reuse that estimate for all requests; set an output token limit
D) Call the Bedrock token-estimation API (CountTokens) for the selected model with the assembled request; prune the lowest-value context until it fits; set an output token limit
explanation: CountTokens gives the model-specific input count that matches actual chargeable tokens, taken AFTER model selection and dynamic context assembly — a shared/generic tokenizer or a static deployment-time estimate can't reliably match per-model tokenization, and summarizing via another FM adds a speculative extra inference call, which is explicitly disallowed.
comparison_note: The 'input side' member of the token/cost trio (011=model routing, 032=output cap sizing): this one is specifically about pre-invocation input-budget enforcement via CountTokens.

question: InvokeModel calls set max_tokens to each model's largest accepted value for every request 'to prevent truncation.' After launch, p95 latency and throttling rose even though generated feedback is usually short, and an EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage-only alarm rarely fires. Need reduced quota pressure and a reliable capacity-planning signal, without changing the FM or going async. Best approach?
options: A) Switch to InvokeModelWithResponseStream, monitor TimeToFirstToken, keep max_tokens at the largest accepted value
B) Request a higher Bedrock token quota, monitor runtime token metrics, use EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage as the PRIMARY planning signal
C) Shorten the system prompt, monitor InvocationLatency, size capacity by comparing EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage against the published token quota
D) Profile Bedrock runtime token and latency metrics, LOWER max_tokens to a validated response cap, treat EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage as a SECONDARY signal
explanation: Throttling reservation is based on input tokens PLUS max_tokens upfront, regardless of what's actually generated — an oversized max_tokens over-reserves capacity even for short completions. AWS documents EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage as an approximation, so it should be a secondary signal, not the primary one. Streaming, quota increases, and prompt shortening are all real levers but none corrects the root over-reservation cause.
comparison_note: The 'output side' member of the token/cost trio (011=model routing, 018=input pruning): this one is specifically about the max_tokens-as-upfront-reservation trap and EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage's documented approximation status.

question: A casework platform (Converse API, tool_use for case updates) needs: raw PII removed before any FM invocation; no raw request/response payloads in Bedrock invocation logging; Bedrock enforcing ZERO durable retention of FM request/response data; sanitized audit records in a versioned S3 bucket fully deleted after 90 days. Best implementation?
options: A) Redact via Comprehend DetectPiiEntities offsets in Lambda before invoking Bedrock; Bedrock data retention = INHERIT; invocation logging disabled; Guardrails on text AND tool_use outputs; S3 Lifecycle Expiration + NoncurrentVersionExpiration

B) Redact via Comprehend DetectPiiEntities offsets in Lambda before invoking Bedrock; Bedrock data retention = NONE; invocation logging disabled; Guardrails on text PLUS custom redaction for tool_use parameters; S3 Lifecycle Expiration + NoncurrentVersionExpiration

C) Mask via Bedrock Guardrails sensitive-info filters; Responses API store=false; ENABLE invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs with KMS; validate tool_use parameters only in the tool service; S3 Lifecycle Expiration + NoncurrentVersionExpiration

D) Scan the audit bucket with Macie; Bedrock data retention = PROVIDER_DATA_SHARE; invocation logging disabled; Guardrails on text plus custom redaction for tool_use; S3 Lifecycle Expiration + NoncurrentVersionExpiration
explanation: Comprehend DetectPiiEntities returns offsets for app-side redaction pre-invocation. Only retention mode NONE guarantees zero durable retention (INHERIT depends on an inherited policy; PROVIDER_DATA_SHARE is explicitly not zero-retention). Guardrails sensitive-info filters cover text but NOT tool_use/function-call parameters, so custom redaction is still needed there. A versioned S3 bucket needs BOTH current-version Expiration and NoncurrentVersionExpiration to fully purge after 90 days — an expiration rule alone just adds a delete marker.
comparison_note: Pairs with 027: 014 is about the full privacy-by-design pipeline (retention mode + logging + Guardrails gap + S3 versioning), 027 narrows in specifically on deterministic, reversible pseudonymization with a reidentification map for authorized reviewers.

question: Deposition transcripts contain names/phones/emails and matter-specific witness identifiers (documented pattern). Firm needs: raw identifiers never sent to the FM, the SAME placeholder for the same entity throughout a matter, and authorized reviewers able to restore identities later — no custom/trained ML model. Least operational overhead?
options: A) Bedrock guardrails with managed sensitive-info filters + custom regex, masking actions, rely on guardrail traces for reviewer reidentification
B) Amazon Comprehend PII detection in a preprocessing Lambda, replace detected entities with generic entity-type labels, store the original transcript in encrypted S3
C) Amazon Macie classifies transcript objects in S3, tags objects with sensitive-data findings, routes tagged objects through Bedrock guardrails
D) Lambda preprocessing layer using Comprehend PII detection AND deterministic pattern rules; stores an encrypted PLACEHOLDER MAP; invokes Bedrock with guardrails enabled
explanation: Comprehend covers common PII types, but the firm's custom witness-identifier pattern needs deterministic regex/rules on top. An encrypted PLACEHOLDER MAP (stable per-entity substitution + authorized reversal) is what guardrail masking, generic entity labels, or Macie tagging can't provide — none of those preserve consistent, reversible pseudonyms.
comparison_note: Narrower sibling of 014: same Comprehend-offset-redaction building block, but the differentiator here is a STABLE, REVERSIBLE per-entity placeholder map rather than retention-mode/logging/S3-lifecycle configuration.

question: A medical-device complaint triage app must classify complaints on a low-cost model by default, but any flagged 'adverse' complaint needs review by TWO different FMs in parallel, with a deterministic rule comparing risk scores, attaching reviewer rationales, and routing disagreements to a human queue. Needs explicit retries/timeouts/execution history per complaint, no fine-tuning. Best implementation?
options: A) Bedrock agent exposing classifier/reviewer/escalation action groups, trace collection, return control for tool calls, agent-orchestrated review steps
B) Bedrock Flow with condition nodes after triage, separate prompt nodes for review, a Lambda node to combine scores, flow output as the escalation record
C) Bedrock intelligent prompt routing to select models, invoke two reviewer calls from Lambda, Lambda postprocessor compares scores and prepares escalation records
D) Step Functions state machine calling Bedrock from Lambda tasks, Choice routing after triage, two reviewer tasks in a PARALLEL state, Lambda aggregates scores and enqueues human escalations
explanation: Step Functions provides explicit branching, guaranteed parallel execution, retries/timeouts, and full execution history — the deterministic scoring comparison belongs in Lambda business logic, not in an agent's self-directed tool selection, a Flow's lighter-weight orchestration, or a Lambda-only design lacking workflow-level history and parallel guarantees.

question: A 70GB instruction-tuned LLM deployment to a SageMaker real-time GPU endpoint keeps failing before traffic is accepted: no local instance storage, artifact download exceeds the startup window, and CloudWatch shows the health check expiring during weight loading. Need an AWS-managed pattern reducing custom serving code with LLM-specific throughput tuning. What should the team do?
options: A) Deploy with an LMI container; tune tensor parallelism and continuous batching; benchmark token throughput BEFORE changing startup parameters
B) Deploy with inference components; assign a model-level scaling policy; increase the attached volume; benchmark AFTER creation
C) Deploy a custom DJL Serving container; configure tensor parallelism/rolling batch in serving code; set larger volume and startup timeouts
D) Deploy with an LMI container; set a larger VolumeSizeInGB; increase ModelDataDownloadTimeoutInSeconds; raise ContainerStartupHealthCheckTimeoutInSeconds based on startup logs
explanation: The documented startup failure modes (no local storage, slow download, health-check expiry) map directly to VolumeSizeInGB, ModelDataDownloadTimeoutInSeconds, and ContainerStartupHealthCheckTimeoutInSeconds — these must be fixed FIRST before throughput tuning (tensor parallelism, continuous batching) is even reachable. A custom DJL container solves the same startup issue but with far more owned serving code than the managed LMI path.

question: A Bedrock Flows officiating-guidance workflow takes one InvokeFlow JSON payload (incident, rule excerpts, tone). It must run an evidence-summary prompt first, feed that summary into a ruling-draft prompt, and let production mobile clients use a stable reference while analysts keep editing the draft. Early tests fail when the whole request is wired to every prompt variable. (Select TWO.)
options: A) Connect the evidence Prompt node output to a downstream Object input; rely on runtime validation to parse the generated text into fields
B) Map the input node document into Prompt node inputs using expressions; pass the evidence prompt's modelCompletion into the ruling prompt
C) Publish a tested immutable flow version and invoke the workflow from production clients through an alias targeting that version
D) Invoke the editable flow draft directly from the mobile app; use a naming convention to identify the production-ready draft
E) Create separate flow input nodes for incident, rules, and tone; connect each directly to the matching Prompt node variable
explanation: A flow has exactly ONE flow input node (outputting the whole payload as 'document'); node-input expressions extract the needed parts. A Prompt node's output (modelCompletion) is typed String, not Object — it can feed a downstream prompt variable but shouldn't be treated as structured data without an explicit typed step. Deployment uses immutable published versions + aliases, so production stays stable while a draft keeps changing.

question: A museum conservation Bedrock KB returns chunks from the correct document IDs with reasonable relevance scores, but the content field only has nearby narrative text — never the embedded table values or diagram captions curators ask about. Want to keep using Bedrock KBs, minimizing custom document-processing code. What should the team do?
options: A) Disable chunking so each affected PDF is indexed as one chunk, then sync
B) Apply fixed-size chunking with a larger overlap for the affected PDFs, then sync
C) Parse the affected PDFs with Bedrock Data Automation or foundation-model parsing, then sync
D) Switch to Hybrid search with a textual reranker, then retest with Retrieve
explanation: A reasonable relevance score from the right document only proves the returned chunk is topically relevant — it doesn't prove the needed facts were ever extracted. Since the facts are simply absent from retrieved content, this is a PARSING problem (default text parser missing tables/captions), not a chunking or ranking problem — chunk-size tuning, hybrid search, and reranking can't recover content that was never indexed.

question: A ConverseStream shipment-planning assistant executes tools (vessel schedules, port restrictions, weather) client-side inside the app VPC. Need an operational framework measuring tool call frequency/failures/latency alongside token usage, model latency, throttles, and streaming responsiveness — with anomaly baselines by customer and workflow, and same-account/Region invocation logs. Best approach?
options: A) Keep client-side tool execution; add customer/workflow values to requestMetadata; instrument each ToolUseBlock and tool result in the app; combine invocation logs with AWS/Bedrock runtime metrics
B) Keep client-side tool execution; set toolChoice=any for all requests; baseline usage from EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage; use TimeToFirstToken as the primary tool-utilization metric
C) Keep client-side tool execution; enable model invocation logging only; infer tool utilization from ModelInvocationLog token fields; use InvocationLatency for tool latency baselines
D) Move tools to server-side tool use on the Responses API; rely on Bedrock to invoke each tool; use model invocation logging to capture customer/workflow baselines
explanation: With client-side tool use, only the application knows tool duration/failures/retries — it must instrument each ToolUseBlock/result itself. requestMetadata is the correlation key for customer/workflow baselines in invocation logs. Token counts and InvocationLatency describe MODEL behavior, not tool execution, so they can't substitute for tool-level instrumentation; forcing toolChoice=any distorts natural tool-selection patterns; server-side tool use via the Responses API is a different execution model not used here.

question: A GenAI incident-reporting app in AWS GovCloud (US-West) uses a custom imported text model, expects predictable quarterly high-usage periods, and requires staying in GovCloud, avoiding long-term capacity commitments, and using the Bedrock runtime API (not operating model servers). Best deployment?
options: A) Deploy to a SageMaker real-time endpoint, put a Lambda function in front, invoke via the Lambda API
B) Create a cross-Region inference profile for the custom model, route through it, monitor throttling with Bedrock runtime CloudWatch metrics
C) Create Provisioned Throughput for the custom model WITHOUT a commitment duration, wait until InService, invoke the provisionedModelArn via bedrock-runtime
D) Create Provisioned Throughput with a ONE-MONTH commitment, wait until InService, invoke the custom model ARN via bedrock-runtime
explanation: In AWS GovCloud (US-West), Provisioned Throughput is documented as supported only for custom models with NO-COMMITMENT purchase — a OneMonth commitment violates both the GovCloud constraint and the 'avoid long-term commitments' requirement. Inference must use the returned provisionedModelArn as modelId, not the underlying custom model ARN. Cross-Region inference profiles route across Regions (breaking the GovCloud-only boundary) and don't support Provisioned Throughput; SageMaker endpoints require operating model servers, which is explicitly disallowed.

question: A public REST API needs synchronous multi-turn browser chat against Bedrock text models without the client contract changing when the supported model changes, plus an async path for large image-caption review jobs (high throughput, must tolerate duplicate delivery). Must reject malformed bodies/missing fields/nonnumeric settings before invoking Lambda. Best implementation?
options: A) REST body models for required fields/numeric settings; InvokeModel from the chat Lambda with ONE SHARED message payload across models; SQS standard queue; idempotent workers
B) REST REQUIRED QUERY PARAMETERS for generation settings; Converse from the chat Lambda; SQS standard queue; rely on the validator to reject nonnumeric QUERY values
C) REST body models for required fields/numeric settings; Converse from the chat Lambda; SQS standard queue; make workers idempotent BEFORE DELETING MESSAGES
D) REST body models for required fields/numeric settings; Converse from the chat Lambda; SQS standard queue; TREAT THE VISIBILITY TIMEOUT AS SUCCESSFUL PROCESSING
explanation: Converse (not model-specific InvokeModel payloads) keeps the client contract stable across model changes. API Gateway REST body-model validation checks JSON types (including numeric fields) BEFORE Lambda; query-parameter validation only checks presence/non-blank, not type. SQS standard queues give at-least-once delivery, so workers must be idempotent AND must delete the message after successful processing — visibility timeout only hides a message temporarily, it's not equivalent to completion.

question: An online brokerage wants centrally enforced Bedrock Guardrails across several AWS Organizations accounts (with one Region approved today, more to follow), while letting trading/compliance apps ADD stricter request-level controls, plus detailed request/response evidence for supported runtime invocations. (Select TWO.)
options: A) Add an automated reasoning policy to the centrally approved guardrails; attach org-level enforcement policies; use app-specific guardrails only for exceptions that RELAX the baseline

B) Create centrally approved guardrails in the management account per required Region, publish FIXED guardrail versions; attach AWS Organizations Bedrock policies to target OUs/accounts referencing those regional versions

C) Configure resource-based policies on the centrally approved guardrails for member accounts; grant invoking roles permission to apply guardrails; enable Bedrock model invocation logging per account/Region to same-account/same-Region destinations
D) Create ONE centrally approved guardrail in the management account, attach one org policy to all OUs, reference the DRAFT version, use the same guardrail ARN for every approved Region
E) Configure account-level enforced guardrails in every member account; require each app to include the guardrail ID/version; use CloudTrail as the ONLY evidence source
explanation: AWS Organizations Bedrock policies are Region-specific and require a FIXED (versioned, not draft) guardrail reference per approved Region — a single ARN can't cover multiple Regions. Enforced guardrails in the management account need resource-based policies granting member-account access, plus invoking-role permission to apply them; app-level guardrails can only ADD stricter controls (union semantics), never relax the baseline. Automated reasoning policies are unsupported in enforced guardrails. CloudTrail alone lacks payload-level evidence — model invocation logging is the separate feature for that.

question: A Maven Java 8 Bedrock service must move to Java 17 this quarter, gain unit-test coverage for request builders, and catch common security issues before code review — using supported local IDEs, minimal custom automation, engineers keeping final control of code changes. (Select TWO.)
options: A) Use Amazon Q Developer in the IDE for Bedrock API code suggestions, generate unit-test scaffolding, and run security scans before opening pull requests
B) Run the Amazon Q Developer Agent for code transformation from a supported IDE to upgrade the Maven Java 8 project to Java 17, then review proposed changes
C) Create an Amazon Q Developer customization from approved repositories, then rely on customized suggestions to perform the migration and security review
D) Build a Bedrock Flows workflow that prompts a foundation model to rewrite Java files, generate tests, and summarize scan findings
E) Create an Amazon Q Business application with internal documentation connectors and plugins, use it as the primary assistant for repository refactoring
explanation: Amazon Q Developer's IDE features (code suggestions, test scaffolding, security scans) and its dedicated Code Transformation Agent (automated, developer-reviewed Java version upgrades) are the two purpose-built, low-overhead tools here. A customization only improves suggestion relevance — it doesn't perform migration or scanning; Bedrock Flows requires building custom orchestration; Amazon Q Business is an enterprise knowledge assistant, not an IDE/refactoring tool.
group: Amazon Q Developer for Code Migration

question: A biomedical device manufacturer drafts field-incident responses via Bedrock/Lambda. Regulators need exact prompt+response evidence per released draft, but the evidence store must not contain raw patient identifiers. Also need near-real-time policy-violation detection on input AND output, block release, and route to a reviewer — no custom ML models. Best implementation?
options: A) CloudTrail for Bedrock API activity to S3, CloudWatch alarms for invocation errors, route alarms to reviewers
B) Deploy on SageMaker real-time endpoint, enable Model Monitor + Clarify, log endpoint payloads to S3, send drift alerts
C) Comprehend + pattern-based redaction in the Lambda workflow, apply Bedrock Guardrails to inputs/outputs, log ONLY redacted evidence, trigger a Step Functions review workflow for violations
D) Enable Bedrock model invocation logging, store prompts/responses in S3, scan the bucket with Macie, notify reviewers after Macie findings
explanation: Redaction must happen BEFORE evidence is written (inline), not after storage — CloudTrail lacks payload content, SageMaker Monitor/Clarify don't provide Bedrock policy filtering, and Macie-after-storage means raw identifiers were already retained, violating the 'no raw identifiers in evidence store' requirement. Guardrails enforce input/output policy in near-real-time; Lambda + Step Functions handles the block-and-route workflow.
comparison_note: Same 'redact-before-storage, never scan-after-storage' principle as 075 and as batch-1's 014/027, but this scenario adds the specific twist of near-real-time BLOCKING + a Step Functions review-routing workflow on top of redaction.

question: A hotel webhook-to-itinerary-summary assistant (API Gateway + Lambda + Bedrock) receives partner messages sometimes containing loyalty IDs, payment references, and API secrets. Need: sensitive values kept out of prompts when possible, misuse/content policy enforcement on input AND output, and ONLY JSON matching a strict mobile-workflow contract returned — layered managed controls, minimal custom ML. (Select TWO.)
options: A) API Gateway request validation w/ JSON Schema + AWS WAF regex pattern sets to reject malformed requests/likely secret formats
B) Preprocessing Lambda using Comprehend PII detection + deterministic pattern matching to redact sensitive values BEFORE invoking Bedrock
C) Amazon Macie discovery jobs on archived transcript buckets, EventBridge alerts on stored sensitive data
D) Apply Bedrock Guardrails to runtime calls, AND have Lambda validate/filter the generated JSON before API Gateway returns the response
E) Configure Guardrails sensitive-info filters + instruct the model to always emit the required JSON shape
explanation: Layered defense needs three stages: pre-inference redaction (Comprehend + deterministic patterns for partner-specific secret formats), runtime Guardrails policy enforcement, and a deterministic Lambda POST-inference JSON-schema validator — prompt instructions alone aren't a reliable machine-contract guarantee, and perimeter-only (WAF/API Gateway) or after-the-fact (Macie) controls miss live prompt content and generated-output validation respectively.
comparison_note: Same inline-redaction-before-invocation principle as 036, but adds the deterministic POST-inference JSON validation step since this scenario's output must exactly match a machine-consumed contract.

question: A game studio's Bedrock assistant drafts replies to player reports. For DRAFT REPLIES: most conservative blocking for Hate/Insults/Violence/Misconduct, but block Sexual content only at highest classification confidence (plot descriptions often have benign romance). For REPORT TEXT: most conservative protection against prompt attacks. No separate moderation model. Best guardrail config?
options: A) Response content filters HIGH for Hate/Insults/Violence/Misconduct, response Sexual = LOW, input Prompt Attack = HIGH
B) Denied topics for Hate/Insults/Violence/Misconduct/Sexual, input Prompt Attack = HIGH
C) INPUT content filters HIGH for Hate/Insults/Violence/Misconduct/Prompt Attack, response Sexual = LOW
D) Response content filters MEDIUM for Hate/Insults/Violence/Misconduct, response Sexual = HIGH, input Prompt Attack = HIGH
explanation: HIGH filter strength is the MOST conservative — it blocks LOW+MEDIUM+HIGH confidence content; LOW blocks only HIGH-confidence content. So Hate/Insults/Violence/Misconduct need HIGH (most conservative), Sexual needs LOW (only block highest-confidence to avoid over-blocking benign romance), and both filters must apply to the correct SIDE — response filters for draft replies, input Prompt Attack for report text. Denied topics are for contextual themes, not predefined categories with confidence thresholds.
group: Guardrails: Filter Strength, Pre-Inference Blocking & Automated Reasoning
comparison_note: Anchors the guardrails trio with 054 (ApplyGuardrail placement/pre-inference blocking) and 044 (Automated Reasoning checks layered on top of the same filter categories) — this question isolates the HIGH-vs-LOW filter-strength semantics specifically.

question: A live-show viewer-question assistant (AppSync + Lambda) must block harassment/sexual/violent-threat/market-manipulation-phrase/prompt-injection content BEFORE a rejected message can influence generated content. Compliance updates market-manipulation phrases several times daily; each request needs an inline decision; audit records must NOT retain full viewer text. Best implementation?
options: A) Lambda resolver reads active phrase-policy version from DynamoDB, calls ApplyGuardrail BEFORE Converse, writes only moderation metadata, invokes Converse only after allow
B) Lambda resolver reads phrase rules PACKAGED WITH THE FUNCTION, passes a guardrail config on Converse, writes only metadata, blocks denied requests
C) Lambda resolver reads phrase rules from DynamoDB, runs Comprehend custom classification, invokes Converse WITH OUTPUT guardrails, writes metadata
D) Synchronous Express Step Functions workflow reads phrase rules from DynamoDB, calls ApplyGuardrail before Converse, ENABLES FULL EXECUTION-DATA LOGGING, returns the decision
explanation: ApplyGuardrail called BEFORE Converse ensures a rejected message never reaches the model. A DynamoDB-backed phrase policy supports several-times-daily updates without redeployment (packaged-with-function rules require a deploy cycle). Output-only guardrails let unsafe input reach the model first. Full execution-data logging in Step Functions would persist full payloads in CloudWatch Logs, violating the 'no full viewer text' audit constraint.
group: Guardrails: Filter Strength, Pre-Inference Blocking & Automated Reasoning
comparison_note: Reuses the ApplyGuardrail-before-inference pattern from batch-1's 004/034, with the added traps of policy-freshness (DynamoDB vs packaged rules) and audit-data minimization (metadata-only vs full execution logging).

question: A pharmacy-benefits single-turn RAG QA feature must: avoid clinical-advice topics, mask member identifiers in prompts/responses, reject answers unsupported by retrieved plan documents, reject answers CONFLICTING WITH MACHINE-READABLE COVERAGE RULES, and keep FM intended-use/limitations documentation. Enforcement before the API returns, minimal custom compliance logic. Best design?
options: A) Bedrock Guardrails w/ denied topics + sensitive-info filters + contextual grounding checks; model-card docs; Lambda gate rejects grounding/topic failures
B) Lambda response gate using Comprehend entity detection + regex + a coverage-rule engine; model-card docs; reject restricted-topic/identifier matches
C) Bedrock Guardrails w/ denied topics + sensitive-info filters + contextual grounding checks + AUTOMATED REASONING CHECKS; model-card docs; Lambda gate rejects failed checks
D) Bedrock model evaluation jobs w/ reference contexts + coverage-rule examples; model-card docs; Lambda gate allows only prompts/models from the latest approved evaluation set
explanation: Contextual grounding (option A/C) catches unsupported answers, but only Automated Reasoning checks can validate output against MACHINE-READABLE coverage RULES (formal logic), which grounding checks and a custom Lambda regex/entity engine can't reliably express. Evaluation jobs are offline governance evidence, not a per-response runtime gate.
group: Guardrails: Filter Strength, Pre-Inference Blocking & Automated Reasoning
comparison_note: Completes the guardrails trio: 041 isolates filter-strength semantics, 054 isolates pre-inference blocking + policy freshness, this one isolates the Automated Reasoning checks feature for rule-based (not just grounding-based) output validation.

question: A credit union's loan-dispute review panel wants to see model-generated reasoning (when the model provides it) for multi-turn Bedrock conversations, but must never expose provider-redacted reasoning content. Guardrails already apply to inputs/responses; follow-up turns must reliably continue after review; extra latency accepted only for review-panel cases. Best implementation?
options: A) Route to a reasoning-capable model via Converse; render reasoningContent.reasoningText when present; PRESERVE the returned signature with the full message history; hide redactedContent
B) Route via Converse; decode reasoningContent.redactedContent into display text when reasoningText is absent; OMIT reasoning signatures from saved history; replay only user-visible messages
C) Route via RetrieveAndGenerate; display citations entries as the reasoning trace; pass retrieved references as the next turn's prior messages
D) Route via Converse with Guardrails; display reasoning blocks AFTER guardrail filtering; create a NEW conversation state after each review; resend only the current prompt
explanation: ReasoningContentBlock is a union — reasoningText OR redactedContent, never both; redactedContent is provider-encrypted content for safety and must never be decoded/displayed. The reasoning signature is a tamper safeguard that later Converse turns must include along with the full prior message history, or continuity breaks. Guardrails explicitly exclude reasoning blocks from filtering, and RetrieveAndGenerate citations are source attribution, not a reasoning trace.

question: A telehealth benefits assistant needs a per-release promotion decision informed by whether responses about disability accommodations vs. equivalent non-accommodation benefits differ in completeness/respectfulness across cohorts. Anonymized transcript samples + reference policy excerpts exist; need auditable cohort-level fairness evidence, no custom scoring model. Best approach?
options: A) Prompt Management + Bedrock Flow replay samples against the candidate release, score with an LLM-AS-A-JUDGE FAIRNESS RUBRIC, publish cohort metrics to CloudWatch
B) Same replay setup, score with BEDROCK GUARDRAILS INTERVENTION COUNTS, publish cohort metrics
C) Same replay setup, score with RANDOM REVIEWER SPOT CHECKS, publish cohort metrics
D) Same replay setup, score with AMAZON COMPREHEND SENTIMENT GAPS, publish cohort metrics
explanation: Guardrail intervention counts only reflect blocked/filtered policy violations, not whether otherwise-safe answers differ in completeness or respectfulness across cohorts. Random spot checks lack systematic cohort coverage; sentiment analysis is too coarse a proxy for fairness in benefit guidance. An LLM-as-a-judge rubric is purpose-built for this qualitative, cohort-comparative assessment without building a custom scorer.

question: A streaming service compares 3 Bedrock text models for a synopsis generator using 750 representative prompts (S3 .jsonl). Need an automated, repeatable FIRST-PASS evaluation (before human preference study) using the SAME dataset and task definition per model, saved results, no custom evaluator. Best approach?
options: A) Three automatic model evaluation jobs via CreateEvaluationJob, one per model/inference profile, SAME S3 .jsonl dataset + SAME task type, S3 output + eval role
B) Three automatic model evaluation jobs, one per model, using the BUILT-IN summarization prompt dataset (same task type), S3 output + eval role
C) ONE automatic model evaluation job listing all three models/inference profiles, same S3 dataset + task type, one S3 output config
D) Three automatic model evaluation jobs, one per model, CONFIGURING MULTIPLE TASK TYPES in each job, same S3 dataset, results to S3
explanation: Automatic evaluation jobs support exactly ONE model/inference profile AND one task type per job — so 3 candidate models require 3 separate jobs, each single-task-type. Built-in prompt datasets are randomly downsampled to 100 prompts, which would silently abandon the team's carefully prepared 750-prompt representative set.
group: Bedrock Evaluation Jobs: Dataset & Job-Scope Constraints
comparison_note: Continues the evaluation-job-mechanics thread from batch-1's 013/023/029 with a new constraint pair: custom vs built-in dataset sizing, and reaffirms the one-model/one-task-type-per-job rule.

question: A 4-week PoC compares several chat-capable Bedrock models: minimize per-model client code, measure latency/throttling/token usage from managed telemetry, and quantify answer quality on a held-out prompt dataset before requesting production funding. (Select TWO.)
options: A) Build the PoC harness on Converse or ConverseStream for the chat workflow; collect AWS/Bedrock runtime metrics for latency, throttles, and token counts
B) Build the PoC harness on InvokeModel for the chat workflow; reuse the SAME request body across all candidate models
C) Run StartAsyncInvoke for the chat workflow; retrieve each result later to compare interactive responsiveness
D) Rely on DEFAULT model invocation logging for prompt samples; compare Invocations with submitted attempts to infer throttling
E) Run Bedrock model evaluation jobs against the held-out prompt dataset, using ONE TASK TYPE PER JOB and the evaluation method matching the scoring need
explanation: Converse minimizes per-model request-shape branching (unlike InvokeModel's model-specific bodies). AWS/Bedrock runtime metrics give managed latency/throttle/token telemetry without app-side timing code. StartAsyncInvoke is for async generation (e.g. video), not interactive chat responsiveness. Model invocation logging is disabled BY DEFAULT (not automatic), and Invocations counts only SUCCESSFUL requests — it can't be used as a throttling proxy.
group: Bedrock Evaluation Jobs: Dataset & Job-Scope Constraints
comparison_note: Pairs with 040: 040 focuses on the dataset/job-scope constraints for automatic evaluation; this one adds the Converse-vs-InvokeModel PoC-harness choice and the 'logging is opt-in, Invocations≠all-attempts' telemetry traps on top of the same one-task-type-per-job rule.

question: Six Bedrock prompt templates (each ~80 SME-reviewed evaluation samples) show inconsistent outputs for two claim types after edits. Team must systematically refine prompts using the samples, compare original vs optimized behavior across THREE candidate FMs, no custom evaluation service. Best approach?
options: A) Run simple prompt optimization (OptimizePrompt) separately per template/model; manually compare rewritten prompts against samples
B) Create an ADVANCED PROMPT OPTIMIZATION job with a JSONL dataset for the 6 templates+samples; use an LLM-as-a-judge rubric across the 3 target models; review original vs optimized results
C) Save each revised template as a DRAFT prompt in Prompt management; use the prompt-version JSON comparison view; select the version with the smallest configuration diff
D) Create managed prompt variants in Prompt builder for each template; use Compare variants with test variables; save the best variant as the working draft
explanation: Advanced Prompt Optimization is evaluation-driven and explicitly supports multiple templates (up to 10), samples per template (up to 100), and multi-model comparison (up to 5) with LLM-as-a-judge scoring — matching 6 templates × ~80 samples × 3 models. Simple OptimizePrompt is a single-prompt, single-model heuristic rewrite with NO evaluation-data support. Prompt-version JSON diffing audits configuration changes, not response quality; Prompt builder's variant comparison isn't built for evaluation-driven optimization at this scale.
group: Prompt Optimization Tools: Simple vs Advanced vs Prompt Management
comparison_note: Extends the Prompt Management family from batch-1's 002/007/026 by introducing the distinct Advanced Prompt Optimization API/workflow, contrasted against the lighter-weight Simple prompt optimization and plain Prompt Management comparison tools.

question: A medication-policy assistant invokes Bedrock via BOTH Converse (bedrock-runtime) and the Responses API (bedrock-mantle). Invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs is enabled in-account/Region, but Logs Insights shows only SOME production requests. Need to search prompt/response content, model IDs, caller ARNs, token counts, and a support case ID without duplicating prompt logging in the app. Best approach?
options: A) Route payload-troubleshooting requests through supported bedrock-runtime operations; log to S3 in a CENTRALIZED LOGGING ACCOUNT; support case ID in requestMetadata
B) Route through supported bedrock-runtime operations; log to CloudWatch Logs SAME account/Region; support case ID in requestMetadata
C) Route through the RESPONSES API on bedrock-mantle; log to CloudWatch Logs same account/Region; support case ID in requestMetadata
D) Route through bedrock-runtime operations; add the support case ID TO THE PROMPT INSTRUCTIONS; query captured prompt text from logs
explanation: Model invocation logging only covers supported bedrock-runtime calls (Converse/ConverseStream/InvokeModel/InvokeModelWithResponseStream) — calls through bedrock-mantle (Responses API) are NOT captured, which explains the visibility gap. Destinations must stay same-account/same-Region (ruling out a centralized logging account). requestMetadata is the structured caller-supplied correlation field — embedding IDs in prompt text is an anti-pattern that can affect model behavior.
comparison_note: Continues the invocation-logging mechanics thread from batch-1's 001, adding the bedrock-runtime-vs-bedrock-mantle endpoint-coverage gap as the new twist. Pairs closely with 047 (same requestMetadata-vs-header distinction, applied across Converse and InvokeModel) and 051 (same logging feature, applied to troubleshooting prompt-confusion content).

question: A tutoring platform uses ConverseStream (chat) and InvokeModel (image feedback) across two Regions. Need CloudWatch dashboards for latency/throttling/tokens/prompt-caching PLUS forensic records filterable by tenant ID and lesson ID. Some payloads exceed 100KB; some responses include binary image data. No custom request logger; all logging destinations stay in the workload account/Region. Best design?
options: A) Invocation logging in each Region, CLOUDWATCH LOGS DELIVERY ONLY; identifiers as requestMetadata on ConverseStream + header on InvokeModel; dashboards from AWS/Bedrock metrics + inline log bodies
B) Invocation logging w/ CloudWatch Logs + S3; identifiers as THE REQUEST METADATA HEADER on ALL Bedrock runtime calls; dashboards from AWS/Bedrock metrics
C) Invocation logging w/ CloudWatch Logs + S3; identifiers as requestMetadata on ConverseStream + header on InvokeModel (correct split); dashboards built from AGGREGATED INVOCATION LOG RECORDS ONLY
D) Invocation logging w/ CloudWatch Logs + S3; identifiers as requestMetadata on ConverseStream + header on InvokeModel; dashboards from AWS/Bedrock RUNTIME AND DELIVERY METRICS
explanation: S3 delivery is required for >100KB bodies and binary image data (CloudWatch Logs caps inline JSON). The metadata mechanism differs by API family: Converse/ConverseStream use the requestMetadata request-BODY field, while InvokeModel/InvokeModelWithResponseStream use the request-metadata HTTP HEADER — using one mechanism for all calls (option B) is wrong. Dashboards need the dedicated AWS/Bedrock runtime+delivery CloudWatch metrics — invocation log records alone aren't a substitute for latency/throttle/prompt-caching metric dashboards.
comparison_note: Same requestMetadata-field-vs-header split as 046/051, but this question's differentiator is the S3-required-for-large/binary-payloads rule plus metrics-vs-log-records for dashboarding.

question: Versioned Bedrock Prompt management prompts (invoked via managed ARN + Converse + promptVariables) sometimes mix policy instructions in production output, and a downstream parser rejects malformed JSON. Need troubleshooting controls exposing actual request/response payloads for FAILED invocations, plus response-format-drift detection, minimal custom telemetry, no AgentCore agents. (Select TWO.)
options: A) Add Lambda application logs for prompt variable keys/request IDs/parser exceptions; rely on those INSTEAD OF Bedrock model invocation logging
B) Use AWS/Bedrock CloudWatch metrics (InputTokenCount, InvocationLatency) to inspect prompt text and response bodies for failed requests
C) Enable Bedrock model invocation logging for bedrock-runtime calls to CloudWatch Logs, AND configure Amazon S3 large-data delivery in the same account/Region
D) Configure structured outputs for the Converse request via outputConfig.textFormat with a SUPPORTED JSON Schema subset for the response contract
E) Invoke the managed prompt ARN with Converse while ALSO supplying system, inferenceConfig, messages, and promptVariables to override the template
explanation: Model invocation logging (not app logs, not CloudWatch metrics) is the only source of actual request/response payloads; large bodies need S3 delivery alongside CloudWatch Logs.
