group: Amazon Q Developer & Q-Family Tool Selection
comparison_note: Same Q-family selection logic as batch-1's 035 and this batch's 037 — this scenario's differentiator is explicitly ruling out a custom-built Bedrock agent as 'too much operational overhead' rather than choosing between Q Developer tiers.

question: A civil engineering safety-review ingestion workflow: PDF checklists w/ tables+signatures, drone images, inspection videos, English toolbox-talk audio (equipment acronyms + employee names), spreadsheet incident logs. Must create reviewable FM-ready text+metadata in S3, preserve document structure, REDACT PII from audio transcripts, normalize spreadsheets, no custom/hosted extraction models. LEAST custom extraction code?
options: A) Bedrock multimodal model from Lambda for PDFs/images/videos/audio; SageMaker Processing converts spreadsheets to the shared JSON schema
B) Bedrock Data Automation for PDFs/images/inspection videos; Amazon Transcribe w/ custom vocabulary AND PII redaction for audio; SageMaker Processing to normalize spreadsheets
C) Amazon Textract for PDFs, Amazon Rekognition for images/videos, Transcribe w/ redaction for audio; SageMaker Processing to merge outputs and generate summaries
D) SageMaker Processing with OCR/CV/speech-to-text libraries for ALL modalities; tabular normalization in the same container
explanation: Bedrock Data Automation handles managed multimodal document/image/video extraction; Transcribe supplies BOTH custom vocabulary (equipment acronyms) AND PII redaction (employee names) specifically for audio — a general multimodal FM prompt (A) lacks those audio-specific controls; stitching Textract+Rekognition+Transcribe (C) requires more custom merge/summarization logic; a fully custom OCR/CV/speech container (D) is exactly the custom-extraction-model overhead the requirement rules out.
group: Multimodal Ingestion via Bedrock Data Automation (Continuation)
comparison_note: Reinforces the 'BDA for documents/images/video + Transcribe (custom vocab + PII redaction) for audio + SageMaker Processing for tabular' pattern from batch-1's 033 and this batch's 072 — same managed-services-over-custom-code principle applied to a third variant of the multimodal-archive scenario.

question: A Bedrock Knowledge Base's S3 data source (text-only interconnection notices) was connected WITHOUT specifying a chunking configuration, and short notices got split across chunks, dropping exception clauses. Source docs are now preprocessed to one-complete-notice-per-file; page-number citations/filtering are NOT needed. Which segmentation approach?
options: A) Create a NEW data source with chunkingStrategy SEMANTIC; sync preprocessed notices; let Bedrock infer notice boundaries
B) Create a new data source with chunkingStrategy FIXED_SIZE; set maxTokens=300, overlapPercentage=20 for the preprocessed notices
C) UPDATE the EXISTING data source to chunkingStrategy NONE; resync the same S3 prefix after replacing objects with one-notice-per-file versions
D) Create a NEW data source with chunkingStrategy NONE; sync the preprocessed one-notice-per-file S3 prefix; retire the original data source
explanation: chunkingStrategy NONE treats each preprocessed file as exactly one chunk — the right fit once file boundaries ARE the desired retrieval unit. But the chunking strategy CANNOT BE CHANGED after a data source is connected (ruling out C, which tries to update the existing source) — a NEW data source must be created, synced, and the old one retired. FIXED_SIZE still risks splitting notices across a token window even with overlap; SEMANTIC delegates boundary decisions to Bedrock instead of using the team's authoritative preprocessing.

question: An e-discovery platform drafts privilege-review recommendations. Low-confidence ones stop until an attorney approves/rejects via an internal HTTPS portal (reviews up to 45 DAYS). Must preserve execution history for audit, NOT keep Lambda running during review. The workflow runs in the case-management account; the firm usually hosts APIs in a CENTRAL PLATFORM account. Best implementation?
options: A) Standard Workflow w/ a WAIT STATE LOOP; Lambda sends the review request, checks a DynamoDB decision item after each wait interval
B) EXPRESS Workflow w/ a Lambda callback integration; pass $$.Task.Token; an API-Gateway-backed Lambda calls SendTaskSuccess/Failure
C) Standard Workflow w/ a Lambda callback integration; pass $$.Task.Token; an API-Gateway-backed Lambda IN THE CASE-MANAGEMENT ACCOUNT calls SendTaskSuccess/Failure
D) Standard Workflow w/ a Lambda callback integration; pass $$.Task.Token; the CENTRAL PLATFORM ACCOUNT'S API Lambda calls SendTaskSuccess/Failure DIRECTLY
explanation: Standard Workflows support durable multi-week waits (Express is capped, ruling out B for a 45-day review). Task tokens MUST be returned by a principal in the SAME AWS ACCOUNT as the workflow — since the workflow runs in the case-management account, the callback Lambda must also be there (C), NOT in the central platform account (D), even though that's where APIs are usually hosted. Wait-state polling (A) adds unneeded delay/complexity versus the direct callback resume.
group: Step Functions Human-Approval Callback (Cross-Account & Duration Limits)
comparison_note: Near-identical scenario to batch-1's 003/017 (same-account task-token rule, Standard-vs-Express duration limit) — this question adds the twist of an organizational norm (APIs usually hosted centrally) that must be overridden to satisfy the same-account callback constraint.

question: A production Bedrock Prompt Management version was stable for months. After draft edits, regression runs show inconsistent output. THREE candidate draft variants differ in instructions, target FM, AND inference settings. Team wants to identify what changed from the deployed snapshot AND run a controlled comparison of the three candidates with the SAME variable values — no custom harness, no single heuristic rewrite. (Select TWO.)
options: A) Run simple prompt optimization (OptimizePrompt) for each candidate with the regression samples, targeting all three models; choose the highest scorer
B) Invoke the managed prompt through Converse w/ promptVariables PLUS system and inferenceConfig overrides; compare outputs from regression runs
C) Use Prompt management VERSION COMPARISON to compare the production version with the current draft JSON; inspect highlighted template/configuration differences
D) Create a single Prompt builder comparison with the production version AND all three candidates (four-way); select the best of the four outputs
E) Configure the three candidates as Prompt builder VARIANTS with shared test variables, run the comparison, save the preferred candidate as the working draft
explanation: Version comparison (C) is the documented tool for isolating what changed from a deployed snapshot — showing highlighted JSON diffs between production and draft. Prompt builder's variant comparison (E) supports up to THREE variants with shared test variables — exactly matching three candidates, but a four-way run combining production+3-candidates (D) exceeds that limit. Simple OptimizePrompt (A) is a single-model heuristic rewrite without evaluation-data or multi-model support; Converse with a managed prompt cannot include system/inferenceConfig overrides (B) — those live in the managed prompt itself.
comparison_note: Same Prompt Management tooling family as this batch's 063/092, but this question is specifically about the version-comparison-for-diagnosis-plus-Prompt-builder-for-controlled-comparison COMBINATION, rather than Advanced Prompt Optimization or a Converse/API-compatibility trap.

question: Two Bedrock workloads: patient-education chat (bursty, on-demand OK, must stay within US COMMERCIAL Regions) and clinical documentation (custom model, stable high volume, needs DEDICATED capacity). SCP currently allows Bedrock invocation only from the application Region; security will approve additional US destination Regions IF the architecture requires them. App must use the correct modelId for each mode. Best architecture?
options: A) US GEOGRAPHY cross-Region profile for chat; SCP/IAM LIMITED TO THE APPLICATION REGION; invoke the custom model via its PROVISIONED THROUGHPUT ARN
B) US geography cross-Region profile for chat; SCP/IAM allow ALL destination Regions in that profile; invoke the custom model by its CUSTOM MODEL ID
C) US geography cross-Region profile for chat; SCP/IAM allow ALL destination Regions in that profile; invoke the custom model via its PROVISIONED THROUGHPUT ARN
D) GLOBAL cross-Region profile for chat; SCP/IAM allow all destination Regions; invoke the custom model via its Provisioned Throughput ARN
explanation: A US GEOGRAPHY profile (not Global, which spans ALL commercial Regions worldwide, violating the US-only requirement) matches the residency constraint. The SCP/IAM must allow ALL destination Regions IN THAT PROFILE — leaving policy limited to only the application Region (A) causes failures. For dedicated capacity on a custom model, the invocation identifier is the returned PROVISIONED THROUGHPUT ARN, not the custom model ID (B uses the wrong identifier).
group: Cross-Region Inference Profile Types & Custom Model Invocation IDs
comparison_note: Same Global-vs-Geographic-profile-plus-SCP-condition family as this batch's 062 and batch-1's 022 (GovCloud Provisioned Throughput) — this scenario combines BOTH the profile-geography trap and the Provisioned-Throughput-ARN-vs-model-ID trap in one question.

question: A legal-aid intake Bedrock agent returns natural-language answers AND emits tool_use function-call parameters for a scheduling tool. Must block unsafe content in prompts+responses, mask PII in text responses, and prevent UNREDACTED PII from being stored in invocation logs OR passed in tool-call parameters. Prefer managed controls, least custom moderation code. Best design?
options: A) Guardrail w/ content filters + custom WORD FILTERS for prompt/response text; add known PII terms via supported text APIs; RETAIN guardrail trace matches
B) Guardrail w/ content filters + DENIED TOPICS for prompt/response text; model PII categories as denied topics; restrict access to ENCRYPTED invocation logs
C) Guardrail w/ content filters + sensitive-info filters; RELY ON GUARDRAIL PII MASKING FOR tool_use PARAMETERS; encrypt model invocation logs
D) Guardrail w/ content filters + sensitive-info filters for prompt/response text; ADD APPLICATION-SIDE REDACTION for tool_use parameters; AVOID RAW model invocation logging
explanation: Sensitive-information filters cover TEXT prompts/responses but explicitly do NOT inspect tool_use function-call output parameters (C's reliance on guardrail masking for tool params misses this documented gap) — application-side redaction is required there. Word filters (A) are exact-match, unreliable for dynamic PII, and guardrail TRACE MATCH fields can retain original PII values — retaining them defeats the goal. Denied topics (B) model contextual THEMES, not individual PII entity types. Encryption (C) protects data at rest but doesn't prevent unredacted PII from being STORED in the first place — avoiding raw invocation logging is the actual fix.
comparison_note: Same sensitive-info-filter-boundary principle as batch-1's 014/027 and this batch's 036/075 — this scenario's specific new nuance is the tool_use/function-call PARAMETER gap (guardrails don't inspect those) rather than plain prompt/response redaction.

question: A regional bank standardizes GenAI gateway deployment via CodePipeline/CodeBuild. Must expose a CONSISTENT Bedrock chat abstraction when models support message-based interactions, publish prompt-test outcomes as NATIVE CodeBuild test reports (no custom parsers), and trigger a compliance workflow from pipeline/stage/action STATE CHANGES without polling CodePipeline. Best implementation?
options: A) Gateway calls Converse/ConverseStream for supported chat models, InvokeModel for model-specific payloads; buildspec report groups collect JUNIT XML files; use PipelineDuration/FailedPipelineExecutions ALARMS to trigger compliance
B) Same gateway; buildspec report groups collect GENERIC JSON prompt test files; EventBridge rules for CodePipeline state-change events
C) Same gateway; buildspec report groups collect JUNIT XML files; EVENTBRIDGE RULES for CodePipeline pipeline/stage/action state-change events
D) Gateway calls InvokeModel FOR ALL chat models, normalizing provider-specific payloads in Lambda; buildspec collects JUnit XML; EventBridge rules for state changes
explanation: Converse/ConverseStream is the standardized chat abstraction (reserving InvokeModel for genuinely model-specific needs, unlike D's all-InvokeModel approach requiring custom normalization). CodeBuild report groups require a SUPPORTED format like JUnit XML — generic JSON (B) isn't documented as valid. EventBridge rules for aws.codepipeline state-change EVENTS are the documented event-driven trigger — CloudWatch metrics like PipelineDuration/FailedPipelineExecutions (A) are narrow operational signals, not state-change event payloads, and can't drive a state-specific compliance workflow.
group: CI/CD Pipeline Observability & GenAI Gateway Abstraction
comparison_note: Companion to this batch's 074 (API Gateway consumer-facing contract via OpenAPI) — both are about exposing a standardized Bedrock interface, but this scenario is about the INTERNAL CI/CD tooling layer (test reports + event-driven triggers) rather than external multi-consumer API contracts.

question: Engineers use Active Directory and need CENTRALLY MANAGED SHORT-TERM access to dev/prod accounts. An ECS task calls the NON-STREAMING Bedrock Converse API through one approved inference profile. Must prevent every account role from invoking UNAPPROVED models. Best design?
options: A) Separate IAM federation in each account; grant bedrock:InvokeModel on ALL foundation models; rely on Bedrock model-access settings
B) IAM users synchronized from Active Directory; attach AmazonBedrockFullAccess to the ECS task role

C) IAM Identity Center with Active Directory; allow the task role bedrock:InvokeModel on the APPROVED inference profile; SCP DENY bedrock:InvokeModel AND bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream on unapproved model AND inference-profile resources
D) IAM Identity Center; grant the task role bedrock:Converse; deny only aws-marketplace:Subscribe for unapproved products
explanation: IAM Identity Center is the centralized, short-term-access mechanism for AD-federated workforce identities — separate per-account federation (A) or long-lived synced IAM users (B) both fail that requirement. bedrock:InvokeModel is the IAM action that ALSO permits Converse (there is no separate 'bedrock:Converse' action, ruling out D). The SCP must deny BOTH streaming and non-streaming invocation actions on unapproved resources — denying only Marketplace subscription (D) leaves the actual invocation path wide open.
group: Centralized Identity & Least-Privilege Model Access (IAM Identity Center)
comparison_note: Same IAM Identity Center + SCP least-privilege pattern as this batch's 066 — 066 focuses on prompt-library-team separation, this one focuses on the bedrock:InvokeModel-covers-Converse identity-action detail plus AD federation choice.

question: An online brokerage compares Bedrock models with a weekly report on successful usage, token consumption, COST attribution from configured application inference profiles, throttling, error rates, and latency percentiles. SREs need to distinguish SLOW FIRST-TOKEN (streaming chat) from SLOW COMPLETION behavior, plus an incident workflow to inspect request/response details for time windows. Most accurate reporting, least custom logic?
options: A) CloudWatch genAI observability + AWS/Bedrock metrics grouped by ModelId; app inference profile cost-attribution view; chart TimeToFirstToken for EVERY runtime call; chart EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage for quota planning; invocation logging for drill-down
B) CloudWatch Logs Insights on invocation logs grouped by model ID; inspect request/response records; derive CUSTOM model-level summaries; publish to a CloudWatch dashboard

C) CloudWatch genAI observability + AWS/Bedrock metrics grouped by ModelId; app inference profile cost-attribution view; chart TimeToFirstToken FOR STREAMING CALLS; chart InvocationLatency for END-TO-END COMPLETION; invocation logging for drill-down

D) CloudWatch genAI observability + AWS/Bedrock metrics grouped by ModelId; app inference profile cost-attribution view; chart InvocationLatency AS FIRST-TOKEN LATENCY; chart Invocations AS TOTAL REQUEST DEMAND; invocation logging for drill-down
explanation: TimeToFirstToken applies ONLY to streaming APIs (A wrongly charts it for every call) — for streaming first-token slowness vs completion slowness, pair TimeToFirstToken (streaming) with InvocationLatency (end-to-end, last-token time). EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage is documented as an approximation, unsuitable as a primary chart. Invocations counts only SUCCESSFUL requests — treating it as 'total demand' (D) ignores throttled/errored requests, and mislabeling InvocationLatency as 'first-token latency' (D) confuses the two distinct metrics.
group: Bedrock Runtime Metrics Semantics (TimeToFirstToken vs InvocationLatency)
comparison_note: Complements this batch's invocation-logging mechanics trio (046/047/051) by focusing specifically on runtime-metric LABELING correctness (which metric measures what) rather than logging destination/payload mechanics.

question: A managed Bedrock knowledge base pilot: supervisors report ambiguous-term searches sometimes return playbook excerpts from the WRONG operational domain. Need a retrieval-quality regression gate: sample recent queries, inspect a candidate set LARGER than default, capture source chunks + Bedrock ranking signal, use a BUILT-IN metric focused on whether retrieved context is relevant. Best approach?
options: A) Call Retrieve w/ vectorSearchConfiguration, overrideSearchType=HYBRID; store retrievalResults content/metadata/score; run a retrieve-only RAG eval w/ Builtin.ContextRelevance
B) Call Retrieve w/ managedSearchConfiguration; SET numberOfRerankedResults ABOVE numberOfResults TO WIDEN candidates; store content+score; run retrieve-only eval w/ Builtin.ContextRelevance

C) Call Retrieve w/ managedSearchConfiguration; choose a numberOfResults value WITHIN THE SUPPORTED RANGE; store retrievalResults content/metadata/score; run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation w/ Builtin.ContextRelevance
D) Call RetrieveAndGenerate w/ managedSearchConfiguration; choose numberOfResults within range; store CITATION content/metadata; run a retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation
explanation: Managed knowledge bases use managedSearchConfiguration (A's vectorSearchConfiguration is wrong for managed KBs). numberOfResults (not numberOfRerankedResults, which reorders — it doesn't expand — the candidate set) is the lever for a larger candidate pool. RetrieveAndGenerate is UNSUPPORTED for managed knowledge bases and its citations don't expose the same score field as Retrieve, ruling out D. Retrieve's retrievalResults score field plus a retrieve-only Builtin.ContextRelevance evaluation directly matches 'built-in metric for context relevance.'
group: Retrieve vs RetrieveAndGenerate for Managed Knowledge Bases
comparison_note: Third of the managed-KB-retrieval family with 083/029/036 — this one isolates the numberOfResults-vs-numberOfRerankedResults distinction and the retrieve-only Builtin.ContextRelevance metric specifically.

question: An energy commodities Bedrock Knowledge Base generates daily risk briefings. Regulators require each factual statement to include SOURCE-BACKED attribution that can be inspected. Ops wants CloudWatch trends for an UNCERTAINTY SCORE the app already calculates. Knowledge base is NOT managed; minimize custom retrieval/attribution logic. Best implementation?
options: A) Invoke RetrieveAndGenerate; render a MODEL REASONING SUMMARY as evidence; publish the app uncertainty score to CloudWatch
B) Invoke RetrieveAndGenerate; render MODEL INVOCATION LOG ENTRIES as audit evidence; publish the app uncertainty score to CloudWatch
C) Invoke Retrieve (not RetrieveAndGenerate); MAP GENERATED SENTENCES TO RETRIEVED CHUNKS manually; publish the app uncertainty score to CloudWatch
D) Invoke RetrieveAndGenerate; render EACH CITATION with its RETRIEVED REFERENCES; publish the app uncertainty score to CloudWatch
explanation: RetrieveAndGenerate IS valid here since the knowledge base is explicitly NOT managed. Its documented citations array (generatedResponsePart + retrievedReferences) is the built-in source-attribution mechanism — reasoning summaries (A) explain model thinking, not source grounding; invocation logs (B) are opt-in operational audit trails, not the citation structure; manually mapping sentences to chunks via Retrieve alone (C) rebuilds attribution logic the managed citation feature already provides. The app's own uncertainty score stays a custom CloudWatch metric — Bedrock runtime metrics aren't a confidence measure.
group: Retrieve vs RetrieveAndGenerate for Managed Knowledge Bases
comparison_note: Fourth of the managed-vs-non-managed-KB retrieval family (083/103/036) — this is the one scenario where RetrieveAndGenerate IS the correct choice, because the knowledge base is explicitly non-managed, contrasting sharply with 083/103's managed-KB constraint.

question: A credit union revises a loan-explanation system prompt and wants to detect whether it produces MATERIALLY DIFFERENT empathy/completeness/discouraging-language levels for otherwise-equivalent applicants across PROTECTED-CLASS PROXY COHORTS. Has an offline dataset w/ cohort tags + reference facts. Must run pre-deployment, preserve prompt version history, no custom fairness classifier. Best approach?
options: A) Store each prompt variant in Prompt Management; run an offline eval workflow w/ an LLM-AS-A-JUDGE evaluator across the cohort-tagged dataset; publish COHORT DISPARITY scores as CloudWatch custom metrics
B) Attach the same Bedrock Guardrail to each variant; configure topic filters/word filters/PII masking; compare GUARDRAIL INTERVENTION COUNTS across the cohort dataset in CloudWatch
C) Store each variant in Prompt Management; route offline dataset responses to a HUMAN REVIEW workflow; promote the prompt with the LOWEST REVIEWER ESCALATION COUNT
D) Store each variant as FILES IN S3 (not Prompt Management); run an LLM-as-a-judge eval; compare ONLY THE OVERALL MEAN SCORE for each variant
explanation: LLM-as-a-judge scoring cohort-by-cohort (not aggregated into one mean) directly measures the qualitative properties (empathy, completeness, discouraging tone) requested — guardrail intervention counts (B) only reflect policy VIOLATIONS, not quality/tone differences in otherwise-safe answers; escalation counts (C) are too coarse for systematic cohort measurement; and an overall MEAN score (D) can hide real cohort-level disparities even when Prompt Management is used correctly.
comparison_note: Near-identical scenario to this batch's 065 — both use Prompt Management + Bedrock Flow/offline-eval-workflow + LLM-as-a-judge fairness rubric + CloudWatch cohort metrics, reinforcing that guardrail counts, spot checks, and aggregate means are all documented anti-patterns for fairness measurement.

question: A university advising Bedrock agent looks up degree requirements AND submits course-substitution requests. Tests show it usually picks the right tool but sometimes sends invalid department codes, omits an advisor approval ID for grad students, or RETRIES AFTER A TIMEOUT creating DUPLICATE submissions. Keep managed agent planning, make the tool contract REUSABLE for future agents, prevent invalid/duplicate writes. (Select TWO.)
options: A) Add few-shot examples to agent instructions showing valid codes, grad approval cases, timeout retry behavior
B) Enable long-term memory to store previous advising context, department preferences, advisor approval IDs across sessions
C) Proxy the student information system through API Gateway request validation; Lambda only forwards accepted requests
D) Define the action-group contract with an OpenAPI SCHEMA in S3 specifying operations, required fields, parameter descriptions, allowed values
E) Implement a LAMBDA action-group HANDLER that validates CROSS-FIELD RULES, checks IDEMPOTENCY before writes, returns structured errors for rejected requests
explanation: The OpenAPI schema (D) gives the agent a precise, REUSABLE contract improving tool selection/argument construction across future agents. The Lambda handler (E) is where deterministic cross-field validation (e.g., grad-student approval ID) AND idempotency checks (preventing duplicate writes on timeout-retries) must live — model outputs are probabilistic, so prompt examples (A) can't guarantee compliance; memory (B) preserves context, not validation; and a thin API-Gateway proxy (C) can't enforce cross-field business rules or idempotency.
comparison_note: Near-identical scenario to this batch's 058 (turbine/CMMS agent) — same OpenAPI-schema-plus-Lambda-handler-validation answer pattern, with idempotency (duplicate-write prevention on retry) as the added twist here versus 058's field-limit/priority-value validation focus.

question: A maritime firm standardizes architecture reviews for GenAI copilots across accounts: needs AWS-maintained best practices, internal requirements (prompt catalogs, conversational interfaces), account-level SHARING of review criteria, and CONTROLLED ROLLOUT of substantial criteria changes. App infrastructure stays on existing CI/CD. Best approach?
options: A) Define workloads in WA Tool; add the AWS-maintained Lens Catalog lens for the workload type; publish internal JSON as MAJOR custom-lens versions; share across accounts; track with milestones/reports
B) Define workloads; use ONLY the automatically-applied FRAMEWORK LENS; import internal JSON with ImportLens; share the DRAFT custom lens across accounts; track with milestones/reports
C) Define workloads; add the AWS-maintained Lens Catalog lens; publish internal JSON as MINOR custom-lens versions; share across accounts; track with milestones/reports
D) Define workloads; REPLACE the AWS-maintained review with an internal custom lens based on COPIED guidance; publish updates as minor versions; share across accounts; track with milestones/reports
explanation: The AWS-maintained Lens Catalog lens supplies official generative AI guidance; a PUBLISHED custom lens (not DRAFT — B's draft cannot be shared or applied to workloads) adds internal criteria. For controlled rollout of SUBSTANTIAL changes, MAJOR versions avoid automatic application to workloads already using the lens — MINOR versions (C, D) are auto-applied, defeating controlled rollout. Copying AWS content into a custom lens as a 'baseline' (D) isn't itself AWS-maintained guidance.
comparison_note: Near-identical scenario to this batch's 056 (restaurant-group version) — both reinforce the same DRAFT-cannot-be-shared and MAJOR-vs-MINOR-version-rollout rules, just with major/minor as the answer-differentiator here instead of the deployment-engine misuse trap in 056.

question: A rail-passenger-support Bedrock assistant handles refunds/rebooking/accessibility. Each message is classified into an intent, then missing fields (route/ticket ID/date) are collected across MULTIPLE TURNS before drafting a response. Sessions can pause up to 12 HOURS and RESUME FROM A DIFFERENT DEVICE. Must keep auditable SERVER-SIDE context, not run compute while waiting. Has an existing Comprehend custom classification endpoint. LEAST custom orchestration code?
options: A) API Gateway/Lambda classifies with Comprehend, stores session state+TASK TOKENS in DynamoDB, uses a Step Functions Standard workflow w/ CALLBACK TASKS for clarification before invoking Bedrock

B) API Gateway/Lambda classifies with Comprehend, stores required fields in DynamoDB, uses LAMBDA FUNCTIONS WITH CONDITIONAL WRITES to manage clarification prompts BEFORE starting a Step Functions Standard workflow for Bedrock

C) API Gateway/Lambda classifies with Comprehend, stores session state in DynamoDB, uses a Step Functions Standard workflow with WAIT STATES that PERIODICALLY RECHECK DynamoDB for missing fields before invoking Bedrock

D) API Gateway/Lambda classifies with Comprehend, stores session state in DynamoDB, PUBLISHES EACH TURN AS AN EVENTBRIDGE EVENT that triggers Lambda continuation handlers for clarification before invoking Bedrock
explanation: The callback task-token pattern (A) lets Step Functions pause durably without running compute, resuming immediately (not via polling) when the next message arrives from ANY device, since state lives server-side in DynamoDB. B pushes slot-filling/turn-transition logic into custom Lambda code instead of Step Functions. C's Wait-state polling adds delay and rechecking overhead vs. direct callback resumption. D uses EventBridge, which lacks the callback semantics for a waiting human interaction — correlation/completion/branching logic would all be custom.
group: Multi-Turn Slot-Filling with Step Functions Callback
comparison_note: Applies the same Step Functions callback-task pattern from the human-approval group (batch-1's 003/017, this batch's 021/096) to a MULTI-TURN CONVERSATIONAL slot-filling use case rather than a single approval gate.

question: A generative product-advice service on ECS/Fargate calls Bedrock during flash sales. A few high-volume TENANTS consume most capacity, some calls fail with retryable exceptions, shoppers abandon after 3 SECONDS. Approved cached answers are reused only if they match tenant + normalized question + catalog version and are <10 MIN old. Must attribute latency across container code AND SDK calls. MOST resilient design?
options: A) Aggressive ECS scaling; ADAPTIVE SDK retries WITHOUT an app-level deadline; SYNCHRONOUS cache refresh before responding; Container Insights + Bedrock metrics for latency
B) AWS WAF rate-based rule BY SOURCE IP; SDK retries until client deadline; serve ANY fresh cache entry for the normalized question; X-Ray traces ONLY from the handler

C) Call a SECONDARY REGION after each failed invocation; IMMEDIATE retries before cross-Region fallback; serve the MOST RECENT tenant cache entry while fallback completes; CloudTrail + X-Ray in the container

D) Enforce PER-TENANT TOKEN-BUCKET admission in the ECS service; BOUNDED SDK standard retries w/ exponential backoff; open a CIRCUIT after failure thresholds; serve only VERSION-MATCHED fresh cache entries; X-Ray traces from the container AND SDK clients
explanation: Per-tenant token-bucket admission (D) protects the shared Bedrock dependency from noisy tenants BEFORE invocation — source-IP rate limiting (B) doesn't reliably enforce tenant fairness. Bounded exponential backoff keeps retries within the 3-second budget (unlike adaptive-without-deadline in A or immediate-retry-before-fallback in C, both of which can consume the whole budget). A circuit breaker provides graceful degradation via the LAST APPROVED matching answer — 'any fresh entry' (B) or 'most recent tenant entry' (C) can cross tenant/question/catalog-version boundaries. Full latency attribution requires X-Ray on BOTH the container AND instrumented SDK clients — handler-only (B) or metrics-only (A) leave gaps.
group: Resilience Patterns: Admission Control, Backoff, Circuit Breaker, Tracing
comparison_note: Same resilience-layering principle (backpressure + bounded backoff + circuit breaker + full-stack tracing) as batch-2's 042, applied here to a multi-tenant fairness scenario with strict cache-key matching rather than a single-tenant pharma summarization endpoint.

question: A university advising assistant uses ConverseStream (chat) and InvokeModelWithResponseStream (summarization) via bedrock-runtime. During incidents, need ONE view correlating latency/TimeToFirstToken/throttles/token+cache usage/log-delivery health/caller identity/per-campus+workflow attribution/prompt+response records (INCLUDING PAYLOADS OVER 100KB)/business KPIs. Managed observability, custom telemetry limited to app-specific KPIs only. Best design?
options: A) S3 as the ONLY invocation-log destination in each account/Region; query invocation records for troubleshooting+attribution; attach request metadata; publish KPIs w/ PutMetricData; dashboards PRIMARILY FROM DERIVED METRICS and CloudTrail

B) CloudWatch dashboards w/ AWS/Bedrock+business metrics; use CLOUDTRAIL MANAGEMENT EVENTS for request-level PAYLOAD visibility+caller audit; attach request metadata; publish KPIs; correlate tenant usage from CloudTrail

C) CloudWatch dashboards w/ AWS/Bedrock+log-delivery metrics; enable invocation logging ONLY TO CLOUDWATCH LOGS in each account/Region; attach request metadata; publish KPIs; QUERY CLOUDWATCH LOGS FOR ALL PAYLOAD TROUBLESHOOTING (including >100KB)

D) CloudWatch dashboards w/ AWS/Bedrock runtime AND invocation-log DELIVERY metrics; enable invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs WITH S3 LARGE-DATA DELIVERY in each account/Region; attach request metadata; publish KPIs w/ PutMetricData; use CloudTrail for API activity
explanation: AWS/Bedrock runtime metrics give the aggregate dashboard view (latency, TimeToFirstToken, throttles, tokens, cache usage) natively — deriving dashboards primarily from raw invocation records (A) adds unnecessary custom processing. CloudTrail answers 'who called what, when' (management/API events) — it does NOT provide prompt/response PAYLOAD visibility (B is wrong). CloudWatch Logs alone caps inline JSON bodies at 100KB (C fails for larger payloads) — S3 large-data delivery is required alongside CloudWatch Logs for full payload coverage. Request metadata handles per-campus/workflow attribution, and custom PutMetricData stays scoped to business KPIs only.
comparison_note: Extends this batch's invocation-logging-mechanics trio (046/047/051) into a FULL layered-observability-design question — same S3-for->100KB and CloudTrail-vs-invocation-logging distinctions, now combined with runtime metrics and custom KPI publishing in one comprehensive scenario.

question: A managed Bedrock Knowledge Base (equipment manuals/safety procedures/playbooks) is shared by multiple internal assistants — some using Bedrock tool use, some a separate MCP adapter. Each assistant chooses its OWN FM, prompt template, response format, citation presentation AFTER retrieval. Shared capability must use retrieval settings VALID FOR MANAGED knowledge bases. LEAST integration risk?
options: A) A retrieval service calls Retrieve w/ managedSearchConfiguration for the managed KB, returns normalized chunks + source metadata
B) A retrieval service calls Retrieve w/ vectorSearchConfiguration and overrideSearchType=HYBRID, returns normalized chunks + source metadata
C) A retrieval TOOL DEFINITION has the FM call Retrieve DIRECTLY, relies on Bedrock guardrails to sanitize returned source references
D) A GENERATION service calls RetrieveAndGenerate for the managed KB, returns generated answers+citations to each caller
explanation: A shared retrieval service using Retrieve + managedSearchConfiguration (A) keeps retrieval decoupled from generation, letting each assistant own its FM/prompts/formatting/citations independently. vectorSearchConfiguration + HYBRID override (B) is the wrong config path for a MANAGED knowledge base. In Bedrock tool use, the MODEL decides a tool is needed but doesn't execute it directly — application code or a supported server-side mechanism does; guardrails don't sanitize retrieved KB references (C misunderstands the execution model). RetrieveAndGenerate (D) both couples retrieval to generation AND is unsupported for managed knowledge bases.
group: Retrieve vs RetrieveAndGenerate for Managed Knowledge Bases
comparison_note: Fifth and final entry in the managed-KB-retrieval family (083/103/104/029/028) — this one applies the same managedSearchConfiguration-required rule to a shared multi-tenant tool-abstraction design, echoing batch-1's Retrieve-for-decoupled-tool-design question (020) but specifically for a MANAGED (not custom) knowledge base.

question: A bank compares two Bedrock FM configurations for email drafting with CLOSE automated scores. Business wants ONE side-by-side evaluation where reviewers rate preference/empathy/brand fit. Has a valid prompt dataset and an S3 results bucket WITHOUT CORS configured. LEAST custom development?
options: A) Configure CORS on the S3 output bucket, create an AUTOMATIC model evaluation job that includes BOTH FM configurations, write results to the bucket
B) Configure CORS on the S3 output bucket, create a HUMAN-BASED model evaluation job that includes both FM configurations, write results to the bucket
C) Leave the S3 bucket UNCHANGED, create TWO automatic model evaluation jobs (one per config), write results to the bucket
D) Leave the S3 bucket UNCHANGED (no CORS), create a human-based model evaluation job including both FM configurations, write results to the bucket
explanation: Automatic evaluation jobs support only ONE model/inference profile per job (A wrongly includes two). Human-based evaluation jobs specifically support comparing TWO models/inference profiles side-by-side, matching the subjective preference/empathy/brand-fit rating need. CORS configuration on the S3 OUTPUT bucket is specifically REQUIRED for human-based evaluation jobs (not automatic/LLM-as-a-judge jobs) — leaving it unconfigured (D) breaks the human-eval workflow.
group: Human-Based vs Automatic Model Evaluation (Multi-Model Comparison & CORS)
comparison_note: New nuance in the evaluation-jobs family (batch-1's 013/023/029, this batch's 040/043): this scenario introduces the human-based-vs-automatic model-count limit (2 vs 1) and the CORS-required-for-human-eval infrastructure detail, neither of which appeared in the earlier automatic-evaluation-focused questions.

question: A pharma RAG assistant already routes each request to the correct domain-specific k-NN OpenSearch index, with shard counts aligned to data-node counts. A new analyst workspace runs 15 INDEPENDENT semantic lookups per page load. Load tests show HIGH CLIENT-SIDE REQUEST OVERHEAD and elevated p95 latency, but data nodes are NOT CPU-bound. No embedding-model change, no index consolidation. Best architecture change?
options: A) Submit the independent k-NN searches through OpenSearch `_msearch`, include `size` in each search body, route each search to its EXISTING target index
B) Submit as SEPARATE requests, INCREASE k in each search body, route to existing target index
C) Submit CONCURRENTLY from the application, include `size` in each search body, REUSE HTTP CONNECTIONS for existing indexes
D) Submit through a SINGLE BROAD k-NN query, include all panel terms in ONE query vector, split returned hits in the application
explanation: Since data nodes aren't CPU-bound, the bottleneck is CLIENT-SIDE REQUEST OVERHEAD from issuing 15 separate round trips — `_msearch` batches multiple independent k-NN searches into ONE request while each search keeps its own target index and body, directly cutting that overhead. Increasing k (B) or reusing connections (C) don't address the per-page request-count problem. Combining all panel terms into one query vector (D) changes retrieval semantics and loses the independence the workspace needs. `size` (not `k` alone) controls actual returned-hit count in each k-NN search body.
comparison_note: Extends batch-2's OpenSearch retrieval-architecture pair (067 hybrid+rerank, 068 index-per-domain+shard-planning) with a THIRD lever: request-level BATCHING via `_msearch` for a scenario where indexing/sharding is already correctly configured and the bottleneck is purely client-side overhead.

question: A clinical-ops assistant coordinates protocol review, feasibility analysis, and checklist generation. Wants OPEN-SOURCE agent code, connections to internal tools exposing MCP endpoints, PRESERVED CASE CONTEXT across turns, and investigations lasting SEVERAL HOURS without managing agent hosting infrastructure. LEAST custom state-management/hosting effort. (Select TWO.)
options: A) Expose MCP tools as OpenAPI action-group schemas in a Bedrock agent; use AgentCore Runtime ONLY as a STATELESS wrapper for the coordinator
B) Implement multi-agent routing MANUALLY inside custom AgentCore Runtime code; pass ALL conversation state in EVERY InvokeAgentRuntime payload instead of reusing sessions
C) Build coordinator+specialist agents with STRANDS AGENTS using its Graph or Workflow COLLABORATION PATTERNS; connect internal tools through NATIVE MCP integration
D) Deploy EACH SPECIALIST AGENT as a separate AgentCore Runtime invocation; generate a NEW runtimeSessionId for EVERY user turn to ensure isolated case handling
E) Deploy the Strands-based agent application to AgentCore Runtime; invoke it with the SAME runtimeSessionId for each request IN A CASE
explanation: Strands Agents is documented as the open-source SDK with native MCP integration AND built-in multi-agent collaboration patterns (Graph/Workflow) — minimizing custom coordination code (C). AgentCore Runtime is the serverless hosting that works with Strands, supports long-running workloads up to 8 hours, and maintains conversation context when the SAME runtimeSessionId is reused across requests within a case (E) — using it as a stateless wrapper (A) or generating a NEW session ID every turn (D) both discard that managed session model, and manually building routing plus passing all state per-payload (B) recreates exactly the custom orchestration the team wants to avoid.
comparison_note: Complements this batch's 060 (MCP server hosting via ECS/Fargate for a DIFFERENT existing containerized server) — this scenario is about choosing the AGENT FRAMEWORK (Strands) and its managed hosting (AgentCore Runtime) with session continuity, rather than hosting a pre-built MCP server behind existing VPC infrastructure.

question: A customs-compliance Bedrock integration (ap-southeast-2) enabled model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs. A document-advice feature calls the RESPONSES API on the `bedrock-mantle` endpoint, but NO invocation log records appear for those requests. Payloads are JSON bodies <100KB. Must capture inputs/outputs for debugging, NO custom logging proxy. Best action?
options: A) Enable CloudTrail data events with advanced event selectors for the feature; use recorded events to review each prompt/response JSON body
B) Switch model invocation logging from CloudWatch Logs to an S3 destination in the same account/Region; keep the feature on the CURRENT endpoint
C) Modify the feature to call a SUPPORTED bedrock-runtime operation such as CONVERSE; continue sending invocation logs to the same-Region CloudWatch Logs destination
D) Monitor ModelInvocationLogsCloudWatchDeliveryFailure in the workload Region; keep the feature on the current endpoint while investigating
explanation: Model invocation logging documentation explicitly states it does NOT currently capture calls through other endpoints such as the Responses API on bedrock-mantle — no destination change (B) or CloudTrail data events (A) fixes an endpoint-coverage gap. Since payloads are already <100KB, CloudWatch Logs is sufficient once the feature moves to a SUPPORTED bedrock-runtime operation like Converse (C). ModelInvocationLogsCloudWatchDeliveryFailure (D) diagnoses DELIVERY problems for covered calls, not an API-coverage gap for an endpoint that was never captured in the first place.
comparison_note: Companion to this batch's 078 — both hinge on bedrock-mantle's distinct behavior from bedrock-runtime; 078 covers discovery-endpoint field sparsity and quota isolation, this one covers the INVOCATION-LOGGING coverage gap specifically, with the fix being to switch the call to a supported bedrock-runtime operation.

question: A 10-day POC for a library patron assistant must support multi-turn chat, STREAM to the browser for perceived responsiveness, switch among chat-capable FMs without rewriting provider payloads, retain prompt/response samples, and report time-to-first-visible-token, full-response latency, tokens, and throttling from MANAGED telemetry. LEAST custom instrumentation?
options: A) InvokeModelWithResponseStream via bedrock-runtime w/ each provider's NATIVE request body; invocation logging to same-account/Region S3 or CloudWatch Logs; monitor streaming+token metrics
B) ConverseStream via bedrock-runtime; invocation logging to same-account/Region S3 or CloudWatch Logs; monitor TimeToFirstToken, InvocationLatency, token-count, throttling metrics
C) Responses API via bedrock-mantle; invocation logging configured to same-account/Region S3 or CloudWatch Logs; compare AWS/Bedrock runtime metrics with samples
D) Converse (non-streaming) via bedrock-runtime; invocation logging same-account/Region; monitor TimeToFirstToken, InvocationLatency, token-count, throttling metrics
explanation: ConverseStream gives BOTH the standardized multi-turn contract (avoiding per-provider payload rewrites, unlike InvokeModelWithResponseStream's native bodies) AND streaming for perceived-responsiveness testing. bedrock-mantle isn't captured by invocation logging at all. Non-streaming Converse can't measure TimeToFirstToken, which applies only to streaming APIs.
group: Standardized Streaming Chat API for Multi-Model POCs
comparison_note: Same converse_stream-plus-start_async_invoke family reasoning as this batch's 080, reapplied here to a pure-streaming-chat POC scenario without an async batch component.

question: An architecture firm's Confluence-backed Bedrock KB must reflect page edits/deletions within 2 hours, skip unchanged pages, and produce an auditable per-refresh-job outcome record. Best maintenance design?
options: A) Scheduled workflow calls StartIngestionJob, treats refresh as successful when GetIngestionJob returns SUCCEEDED
B) Scheduled workflow calls StartIngestionJob for the data source, polls GetIngestionJob until a TERMINAL status is reached
C) Scheduled workflow calls IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments and DeleteKnowledgeBaseDocuments for each changed Confluence page event
D) Scheduled workflow writes page embeddings directly to the vector store and deletes stale vectors by Confluence page ID
explanation: SUCCEEDED is not a valid ingestion job status (the documented success value is COMPLETE) — the workflow must poll GetIngestionJob until any TERMINAL status. Direct document ingestion operations (IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments/DeleteKnowledgeBaseDocuments) are limited to S3 and custom data sources — NOT Confluence connector sources, which must use the sync/ingestion-job path. StartIngestionJob's documented incremental behavior already skips unchanged pages and removes deleted ones, so writing directly to the vector store bypasses managed sync semantics entirely.
comparison_note: Extends the KB data-source mechanics family (this batch's 059/061/073) with the CONNECTOR-vs-direct-ingestion distinction: Confluence (a connector source) must use StartIngestionJob, unlike S3/custom sources which support direct document operations.

question: Storm-damage claim packages (PDFs/photos/work orders/notes) arrive via EventBridge. Must extract claim fields, run fraud scoring+policy checks, require supervisor approval on low confidence/high totals, create a ServiceNow task ONLY after checks/approvals complete. Need per-package workflow history, controlled partner-API retries, MINIMAL custom document parsing. Best implementation?
options: A) Step Functions STANDARD workflow; Textract+Rekognition+CUSTOM LAMBDA PARSERS for extraction; store normalized outputs in S3; branch exceptions to approval; Lambda for ServiceNow
B) EventBridge rule invokes ONE LAMBDA FUNCTION; call Bedrock Data Automation, run scoring, write to S3, request approvals, create ServiceNow task — ALL FROM THE SAME FUNCTION
C) Step Functions EXPRESS workflow; Bedrock Data Automation w/ extraction blueprints; Lambda for scoring; POLL a DynamoDB approval flag; create ServiceNow task after approval
D) Step Functions STANDARD workflow; Bedrock Data Automation w/ extraction blueprints; store outputs in S3; Lambda for scoring AND ServiceNow task creation; branch exceptions to approval
explanation: Bedrock Data Automation with blueprints handles managed multimodal extraction (PDFs, photos, notes) without custom OCR/image-analysis stitching (unlike A's Textract+Rekognition+custom-parser approach). A single Lambda function (B) is a weak fit for approval-driven durable state and auditable retries. Express workflows (C) are a poor fit for approval-driven processes needing long-lived durable state and per-package inspectable history — Standard workflows (D) provide that natively alongside branching and retries.
group: Bedrock Data Automation + Step Functions Standard for Approval-Gated Processing
comparison_note: Reinforces the Bedrock-Data-Automation-over-custom-extraction principle from batch-1's 008/033 and this batch's 094, combined with the Standard-vs-Express durability distinction seen throughout the human-approval-callback family.

question: A match-recap generator (Lambda calling a Bedrock text FM) sees unpredictable spikes; generations take 20-45s, no dedicated capacity wanted. FM is eligible for cross-Region inference across approved US commercial Regions. CloudWatch shows InvocationThrottles; Lambda still uses the DEFAULT timeout; Lambda concurrency is well below quota. TWO changes for LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
options: A) Increase the Lambda timeout to cover the longest expected generation while staying below the 900-second maximum
B) Enqueue recap requests in SQS and run Lambda workers that invoke the PRIMARY-REGION base model asynchronously
C) Invoke the primary-Region base model through an APPLICATION INFERENCE PROFILE configured for usage tracking by workload
D) Submit recap prompts as Amazon Bedrock BATCH INFERENCE jobs with S3 input/output for later retrieval
E) Invoke a CROSS-REGION Bedrock inference profile from the bedrock-runtime endpoint by passing the profile identifier as modelId
explanation: Two SEPARATE limits are visible: Lambda's default timeout (fixed by raising it, up to 900s, option A) controls how long the wrapper waits; Bedrock InvocationThrottles (fixed by adding regional capacity via a cross-Region inference profile as modelId, option E) controls whether the model call itself is throttled. SQS/async workers and application inference profiles (B, C) don't add cross-Region routing capacity; batch inference (D) adds delayed-retrieval overhead unsuitable for a live per-request path.
group: Bedrock Runtime Capacity: Lambda Timeout vs Cross-Region Throttling
comparison_note: Same cross-Region-inference-profile-as-modelId pattern as batch-2's 062/098 and this batch's 149 — this scenario's distinguishing twist is pairing it with the SEPARATE Lambda-timeout fix, since both symptoms (throttling AND wrapper timeout) appear together.

question: A freight forwarder's Converse app summarizes broker notes (<100KB, containing shipper names/phones/passport numbers/driver license IDs) and emits tool_use requests. Bedrock data retention = none; invocation logging DISABLED. Sanitized transcripts stored in a versioned S3 bucket. Need additional controls preventing PII exposure DURING FM interactions AND detecting accidental PII in the STORED ARCHIVE — no custom ML models. (Select TWO.)
options: A) Use Amazon Macie discovery as a SYNCHRONOUS REQUEST FILTER, scanning each submitted transcript object; invoke Bedrock only after discovery returns no PII
B) Configure Guardrails sensitive-info filters to anonymize prompts/responses; rely on the guardrail to remove PII from text AND tool_use output parameters
C) Enable Bedrock model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs+S3; rely on guardrail anonymization to keep raw prompts and guardrail traces free of PII
D) Run Macie AUTOMATED DISCOVERY or TARGETED DISCOVERY JOBS with managed data identifiers on the S3 transcript bucket; route findings to the security remediation workflow

E) Insert a Lambda privacy gate that calls Comprehend DetectPiiEntities, redacts request text from returned offsets BEFORE Bedrock invocation, and blocks/redacts tool_use arguments before tool execution
explanation: Two DIFFERENT paths need two DIFFERENT tools: Macie's managed data identifiers (passport numbers, driver license IDs) are purpose-built for discovering sensitive data ALREADY IN S3 (the archive) — NOT for synchronous per-request filtering (A misuses Macie as a live filter; Macie evaluates on a periodic/job basis). For the LIVE interaction path, DetectPiiEntities returns offsets the app must redact BEFORE invocation, and — since Guardrails sensitive-info filters explicitly do NOT cover tool_use/function-call output parameters (ruling out B and C's reliance on guardrail-only PII handling) — tool_use arguments need separate blocking/redaction in the same Lambda gate.
group: PII Redaction: Live-Path vs Archive-Path Controls (Macie + Comprehend)
comparison_note: Companion to this batch's 121 (same tool set, grocery-chain scenario) — both reinforce Macie-for-archive vs Comprehend-Lambda-gate-for-live-path, but 120 adds the tool_use-parameter gap that 121's simpler text-only scenario doesn't need.

question: A grocery chain's loyalty-feedback summarizer must retain product names/store numbers/dates/complaint categories, but must NOT send raw identifiers (names/phones/emails/addresses/fixed-pattern loyalty IDs) to the FM or return them to analysts — no reidentification needed later, LEAST operational overhead. Best solution?
options: A) Run Macie sensitive data discovery on the S3 feedback bucket BEFORE processing; invoke Bedrock only after tagging sensitive objects and INSTRUCTING THE MODEL to omit identifiers
B) Lambda preprocessor using Comprehend PII detection + a regex for loyalty IDs; apply a Bedrock guardrail ONLY to model RESPONSES after inference
C) Bedrock guardrail w/ sensitive-info filters for PII AND a regular-expression filter for loyalty IDs; apply anonymization to BOTH prompts and responses during inference
D) Bedrock guardrail w/ sensitive-info filters for supported PII; apply anonymization to prompts+responses; handle loyalty IDs through PROMPT INSTRUCTIONS
explanation: A managed Bedrock guardrail combining sensitive-info filters (standard PII) AND a regex filter (custom-pattern loyalty IDs), applied to BOTH prompts and responses, covers the full requirement with the LEAST operational overhead — a custom Lambda+Comprehend preprocessor (B) duplicates functionality the guardrail already provides, Macie (A) doesn't perform inline anonymization for inference requests, and prompt instructions (D) are not a reliable deterministic privacy boundary for arbitrary identifiers.
group: PII Redaction: Live-Path vs Archive-Path Controls (Macie + Comprehend)
comparison_note: Simpler companion to this batch's 120 — same Macie-is-archive-only / Comprehend-or-guardrail-is-live-path principle, but without the tool_use complication, letting the FULLY MANAGED guardrail (regex + sensitive-info filters) win outright over any custom Lambda preprocessing.

question: Several Bedrock chat assistants run from Lambda in one account/Region with invocation logging already enabled to CloudWatch Logs. During an incident, costs rose and users reported low-quality answers. Need a repeatable way to use CloudWatch Logs Insights to find which operations/models/caller-roles produced the largest token volumes, then inspect prompts/responses — WITHOUT duplicate full-body logging in Lambda. LEAST operational overhead?
options: A) CloudTrail Lake queries for bedrock-runtime API events grouped by operation/model/caller role; join with Lambda logs for prompt/response review

B) Saved CloudWatch Logs Insights queries on the Bedrock INVOCATION LOG GROUP filtering ModelInvocationLog records, projecting operation/modelId/identity.arn/token-count; open matching payloads for drilldown
C) Send NEW Bedrock invocation logs to S3, catalog for Athena queries, export incident result sets back into CloudWatch Logs
D) Create structured LAMBDA LOGS beside each Bedrock call writing operation/model/caller role/token counts/FULL PROMPT AND RESPONSE PAYLOADS, query those application logs
explanation: Bedrock invocation logs are ALREADY delivered to CloudWatch Logs with documented fields (operation, modelId, identity.arn, input.inputTokenCount, output.outputTokenCount) — querying them directly with Logs Insights needs zero new instrumentation. CloudTrail lacks these payload/token-count fields; routing to S3+Athena (C) adds an unneeded pipeline when the data is already in CloudWatch Logs; duplicating full-body logging in Lambda (D) is explicitly what the requirement rules out.
group: CloudWatch Logs Insights on Bedrock Invocation Logs
comparison_note: Extends the invocation-logging-mechanics family (this batch's 046/047/051, batch-2's earlier group) with the specific ANALYSIS pattern (CloudWatch Logs Insights queries on the existing ModelInvocationLog schema) rather than logging-destination or metadata-mechanics questions.

question: A delivery network uses Meta Llama 3.1 405B Instruct via a supported US cross-Region inference profile. Retrieved context + explanation often pushes total input+output to ~12K tokens. Operators need FASTER responses during incidents, keep the SAME FM, finance won't approve Reserved capacity or Priority tier. Team wants to reduce prompt-size-related fallback to Standard latency. Best request design?
options: A) Prune context + cap response tokens to fit the supported total token size; send with service_tier=DEFAULT and OMIT performanceConfig.latency
B) Prune context + cap response tokens to fit the supported total token size; send with performanceConfig.latency=OPTIMIZED and leave service_tier UNSET
C) Keep context unchanged; send with service_tier=FLEX, rely on discounted processing for bursts and retry slow responses
D) Keep context unchanged; send with performanceConfig.latency=OPTIMIZED; inspect the served latency configuration in the response and CloudTrail logs
explanation: For Meta Llama 3.1 405B Instruct specifically, Bedrock documents fallback to Standard latency when latency-optimized requests EXCEED a total-token threshold — so pruning context/capping output is the ROOT-CAUSE fix (unlike D, which only observes the fallback without preventing it). performanceConfig.latency=optimized is the request to make (omitting it, as in A, defaults to standard — service_tier=default is a completely separate, irrelevant control). Flex (C) trades speed for cost, wrong for an active-incident console needing faster responses.
comparison_note: Fourth entry in the performanceConfig.latency-vs-service_tier family (batch-2's 038/055/062, this batch's 081) — this scenario's unique twist is the MODEL-SPECIFIC TOKEN-SIZE THRESHOLD that silently falls back to Standard latency unless input is pruned first.

question: Attorneys submit long multi-issue questions against a CUSTOM vector-search KB. Must split each request into smaller searches, return ONLY retrieved chunks+metadata for the app to rank/display (no generated narrative), orchestrate retry+audit across steps. Best approach?
options: A) Step Functions AWS SDK integration calls RetrieveAndGenerate for the original question, parses ONLY the citations, passes cited references to the app
B) Lambda invoked from Step Functions decomposes the question, calls Knowledge Bases RETRIEVE for each subquery via AWS SDK integrations, aggregates the retrieved chunks
C) AgenticRetrieveStream for the existing CUSTOM vector-search KB, set generateResponse=false, use the final deduplicated retrieval results
D) RetrieveAndGenerate with orchestrationConfiguration.queryTransformationConfiguration=QUERY_DECOMPOSITION, discard the generated response before display
explanation: Lambda-based decomposition + per-subquery Retrieve calls (orchestrated by Step Functions for retry/audit) directly returns chunks without any generation step — matching the 'no narrative answer' requirement exactly. AgenticRetrieveStream currently REQUIRES a fully managed knowledge base (ruling out C for this CUSTOM vector-search KB). Both RetrieveAndGenerate-based options (A, D) perform unnecessary model invocation and cost even when the generated text is discarded.
group: Retrieve-Only Query Decomposition for Custom Knowledge Bases
comparison_note: Complements the managed-KB Retrieve-vs-RetrieveAndGenerate family (this batch's 138, batch-2's 083/103/104/111/028/029/036) with the CUSTOM-KB case where AgenticRetrieveStream is explicitly unavailable, forcing a custom Lambda-decomposition-plus-Retrieve pattern instead.

question: A museum curator assistant (Converse/ConverseStream) requests tools for provenance/rights/scheduling, executed in the app's VPC. Need a tool-performance framework correlating tool call patterns across agents with token usage/latency/errors/throttles/streaming responsiveness, baseline-based anomaly detection by collection/agent/workflow, and supported invocation logs available same-account/Region. MOST operationally useful observability?
options: A) Collect ToolUseBlock name/input/toolUseId from Converse responses, enable invocation logging, derive tool success/latency/anomaly baselines ONLY FROM BEDROCK LOG RECORDS

B) Instrument the CLIENT-SIDE tool executor to publish per-tool metrics with toolUseId+agent tags, pass collection/workflow values in requestMetadata, enable invocation logging, correlate with Converse usage and AWS/Bedrock metrics
C) Move tool execution to SERVER-SIDE tool use on the Responses API, enable invocation logging, use logged request records to correlate tool latency with AWS/Bedrock metrics
D) Set toolChoice=ANY for all Converse requests, collect token/latency/throttle/EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage metrics, baseline tool utilization from FORCED tool requests
explanation: With client-side tool use, only the APPLICATION knows real tool execution latency/failures — Bedrock logs (A) can show what tool was REQUESTED but never measure execution after the app calls the internal API. requestMetadata is the documented correlation key for collection/agent/workflow filtering in invocation logs. Server-side tool use (C) is a Responses-API pattern not used here, and forcing toolChoice=any (D) distorts natural tool-selection behavior while EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage remains approximate.
comparison_note: Near-identical scenario to batch-2's 016 (same client-side-instrumentation-plus-requestMetadata answer) — reinforces that Bedrock's own logs/metrics can never substitute for application-side tool-execution telemetry.

question: A rights-management contract-summarization workflow must reject disallowed text BEFORE model invocation, validate generated text before returning it, and route to human review if a call STALLS. Valid calls take 75-100s; the full remediation workflow runs up to 8 MINUTES. Security requires application roles blocked from invoking Bedrock unless the approved guardrail ID+version is supplied. Best implementation?
options: A) Standard workflow, guardrail INPUT+branch on GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED, Bedrock via Lambda w/ 900s Lambda timeout, CLOUDWATCH GUARDRAIL METRICS to stop stalled work, guardrail OUTPUT, IDENTITY ALLOW POLICIES
B) Standard workflow, guardrail INPUT+branch, Bedrock via an HTTP TASK w/ TimeoutSeconds=180, catch States.Timeout, guardrail OUTPUT, explicit Deny on bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier
C) Standard workflow, guardrail INPUT+branch, Bedrock via Lambda w/ ALIGNED Lambda AND Task timeouts, catch States.Timeout for review, guardrail OUTPUT, explicit Deny on bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier
D) EXPRESS workflow, guardrail INPUT+branch, Bedrock via Lambda w/ 900s Lambda timeout, catch States.Timeout, guardrail OUTPUT, enforce access with a PERMISSIONS BOUNDARY
explanation: ApplyGuardrail with source=INPUT (before invocation) and source=OUTPUT (after) validates independently of the model call. An HTTP Task (B) has a HARD 60-second maximum regardless of configured TimeoutSeconds — invalid for 75-100s calls. Standard (not Express, which caps at 5 minutes) is required for an 8-minute remediation window (ruling out D). Lambda AND Step Functions Task timeouts must be explicitly ALIGNED (Task's default is very large) so a Catch on States.Timeout reliably routes stalls to review. CloudWatch guardrail metrics (A) are observability, not a workflow control; identity Allow policies and permissions boundaries (A, D) don't enforce a SPECIFIC guardrail — only an explicit Deny on bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier does.
comparison_note: Near-identical scenario to batch-2's 034 (same HTTP-Task-60s-cap trap, same explicit-Deny-on-bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier enforcement) — this question adds the Lambda-Task-timeout-ALIGNMENT nuance and the Standard-vs-Express 8-minute-duration constraint on top.

question: A travel marketplace runs ConverseStream (bedrock-runtime) AND OpenAI-compatible Responses API (bedrock-mantle). App computes response-quality and hallucination-risk scores post-generation. Must monitor token usage, streaming responsiveness, token-burst anomalies, response-quality drift, PLUS detailed request/response records wherever Bedrock logging can collect them. LEAST custom instrumentation, preserving metric accuracy?
options: A) Endpoint-specific CloudWatch dashboards; AWS/Bedrock runtime latency+token metrics AND AWS/BedrockMantle token+error metrics; publish custom quality-risk metrics; anomaly detection alarms on token metric math AND custom KPIs; enable RUNTIME model invocation logging

B) Endpoint-specific dashboards; documented namespaces for token metrics; custom quality metrics; token-burst alarms ONLY on EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage; enable invocation logging for BOTH endpoint families
C) ONE AWS/BedrockMantle dashboard used for BOTH endpoints; infer runtime responsiveness from token totals; custom quality metrics; enable invocation logging for mantle Responses API calls
D) ONE AWS/Bedrock dashboard used for BOTH endpoints; calculate mantle latency from TimeToFirstToken; store quality scores only as log fields; enable invocation logging for ALL Bedrock endpoints
explanation: AWS/Bedrock (runtime) and AWS/BedrockMantle (OpenAI-compatible) are DOCUMENTED SEPARATE namespaces — using one namespace for both endpoints (C, D) is invalid, and mantle doesn't publish InvocationLatency/TimeToFirstToken equivalents (D's calculation attempt fails). EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage alone (B) is documented as approximate, unsuitable as the SOLE burst signal. Model invocation logging captures only bedrock-runtime calls — 'enable for both endpoint families' or 'all Bedrock endpoints' (B, D) overclaims coverage for mantle.
comparison_note: Extends the bedrock-mantle-distinct-behavior family (this batch's 078/115) into the METRICS-NAMESPACE dimension specifically — same endpoint-isolation principle, now applied to CloudWatch namespaces rather than discovery fields or logging coverage.

question: A prompt-quality troubleshooting pipeline must replay paired requests against CURRENT and CANDIDATE prompt versions, capture ACTUAL request/response payloads plus invocation metadata for BOTH streaming and nonstreaming supported invocations, and do automated output diffing in CloudWatch Logs or S3 — no custom payload-capture code added to every caller. Best approach?
options: A) Enable invocation logging in each account/Region, replay paired requests through the RESPONSES API endpoint, diff the captured records
B) Enable invocation logging in each workload account to a CENTRALIZED S3 bucket in an OBSERVABILITY ACCOUNT, replay through runtime calls, diff the copied records
C) Enable invocation logging in each workload account/Region to SAME-ACCOUNT, SAME-REGION CloudWatch Logs or S3, replay through bedrock-runtime calls, diff the captured records
D) Enable CloudTrail event logging in each account/Region, replay through bedrock-runtime calls, diff the CloudTrail records that contain prompt/completion payloads
explanation: Model invocation logging captures bedrock-runtime calls only (ruling out A's Responses API replay) and its destinations MUST be same-account/same-Region (ruling out B's centralized cross-account bucket). CloudTrail (D) records API activity, not the prompt/completion payloads needed for diffing. Enabling the native feature to same-account/Region CloudWatch Logs or S3 (C) gets the required payloads with zero custom capture code added to callers.
group: Model Invocation Logging for Output-Diffing & Troubleshooting
comparison_note: Reinforces the same-account/same-Region-destination and bedrock-runtime-only-coverage rules from this batch's invocation-logging family (046/047/051/122) — applied here specifically to an output-DIFFING use case rather than dashboarding or incident drilldown.

question: A museum curator assistant filters by collection (exact), optionally matches ANY era tag, and performs NUMERIC RANGE filters on acquisition time. Metadata (collection/curator/eraTags/acquiredEpoch) is maintained by a separate catalog pipeline in its OWN S3 prefix. Best implementation?
options: A) Apply S3 OBJECT TAGS to source objects for collection/curator/eraTags/acquiredEpoch; apply retrieval filters against tag values
B) Create a `filename.extension.metadata.json` file per object in the catalog prefix, configure metadataFilesPrefix; model collection/curator/eraTags/acquiredEpoch ALL AS STRING
C) Write attributes as S3 USER-DEFINED METADATA HEADERS on each source object; configure the KB to use the document prefix, model all headers as metadata attributes

D) Create a `filename.extension.metadata.json` file per object in the catalog prefix, configure metadataFilesPrefix; model collection+curator as STRING, eraTags as STRING_LIST, acquiredEpoch as NUMBER
explanation: S3 object tags (A) and user-defined metadata headers (C) are NOT the documented Bedrock KB metadata mechanism — that's the associated `.metadata.json` file, with metadataFilesPrefix allowing a SEPARATE catalog-managed prefix as required here. The attribute TYPE choice matters: eraTags needs STRING_LIST to support 'match ANY tag' semantics, and acquiredEpoch needs NUMBER to support numeric range filtering — modeling everything as STRING (B) breaks both of those filter patterns.
comparison_note: Reinforces the same `.metadata.json`-file-not-S3-tags principle from batch-2's 059 (CSV single-content-field case), now applied to a document KB with the additional attribute-TYPE-selection nuance (STRING_LIST vs NUMBER vs STRING) that 059 didn't need.

question: Several product-line Bedrock KBs use RDS/MongoDB Atlas/Pinecone/S3_VECTORS with STANDARD FLOAT embeddings. A new program introduces BINARY vector embeddings for SUPPORTED workloads only; teams choose embedding models independently. Need an automated release guardrail preventing unsupported migrations, keeping nonbinary workloads on current stores, favoring SERVERLESS unless an exception accepts cluster administration. Best approach?
options: A) Enable binary embeddings ONLY when the selected embedding model supports BINARY AND storage target = OPENSEARCH_SERVERLESS BY DEFAULT; allow OPENSEARCH_MANAGED_CLUSTER only through an exception; leave other valid targets on float
B) Enable binary when the model supports BINARY across OPENSEARCH_SERVERLESS, RDS, and MONGO_DB_ATLAS after verifying dimensions; leave Pinecone/S3_VECTORS on float
C) Enable binary on OPENSEARCH_SERVERLESS by default and OPENSEARCH_MANAGED_CLUSTER by exception after validating EMBEDDING DIMENSIONS ONLY; leave others on float
D) Enable binary for EVERY valid StorageConfiguration type after validating type names/model IDs/mappings/tenant routing; roll back ONLY IF ingestion/retrieval tests fail
explanation: Binary vector storage is documented as supported ONLY for OpenSearch Serverless and OpenSearch Managed clusters — NOT RDS, MongoDB Atlas, Pinecone, or S3_VECTORS (ruling out B). TWO compatibility checks are required together: the embedding MODEL must support BINARY, AND the storage TARGET must support binary vectors — checking dimensions alone (C) misses the model-support check. This must be a PREDEPLOYMENT policy (A), not a reactive rollback-after-test-failure approach (D). OpenSearch Serverless as the default (with Managed Cluster only via exception) matches the serverless-preference-unless-exception requirement.

question: A field-service warranty RAG feature needs Salesforce case data. Compliance requires a RETAINED COPY of synchronized extracts in S3 for security scanning, refresh at least every 15 MINUTES, minimize custom connector/OAuth handling, and downstream Bedrock ingestion delays must NOT back-pressure Salesforce updates. LEAST custom integration effort?
options: A) Configure a Salesforce connector DIRECTLY in Bedrock Knowledge Bases; EventBridge Scheduler starts ingestion periodically; store CloudWatch logs for audit
B) Configure Salesforce OUTBOUND MESSAGES to an API Gateway endpoint; Lambda writes each payload to S3; INVOKE BEDROCK IMMEDIATELY; rely on API Gateway throttling
C) EventBridge scheduled Lambda POLLS the Salesforce REST API; store queried records in S3; another Lambda starts Knowledge Bases ingestion
D) Amazon AppFlow SCHEDULED FLOW from Salesforce to S3; S3 event notifications ENQUEUE work in SQS; Lambda starts Knowledge Bases ingestion with a DEAD-LETTER QUEUE
explanation: AppFlow is the managed SaaS-to-S3 data movement service, avoiding custom Salesforce API polling/pagination/OAuth-refresh logic (unlike C's hand-rolled polling Lambda). It also gives the REQUIRED retained S3 copy for security scanning — a direct Bedrock KB connector (A) has no such retained landing zone. SQS between the S3 landing zone and Bedrock ingestion (D) decouples the downstream ingestion latency from the Salesforce sync path (unlike B's immediate synchronous Bedrock invocation, which couples the two and risks back-pressure).

question: A utility has 6 outage-notification prompt templates, each with 80 evaluation samples, and wants to optimize/compare across 3 supported Bedrock models. Templates use variables like outageSummary/serviceArea/customerSegment. Must prepare optimization input WITHOUT custom orchestration. Correct input preparation?
options: A) JSONL with ONE EVALUATION SAMPLE per line; repeat templateId/promptTemplate for each sample; use {variableName} SINGLE-BRACE placeholders; rely on the job to group by templateId
B) A SINGLE JSON DOCUMENT with an array of all templates; set version to a current release date; combine ALL variable names in ONE inputVariables object; attach samples under each template

C) JSONL with ONE PROMPT TEMPLATE per line; set version to bedrock-2026-05-14; include templateId/promptTemplate/evaluationSamples; define inputVariables entries whose keys exactly match {{variableName}} placeholders
D) JSONL with one prompt template per line; include BOTH steeringCriteria AND customLLMJConfig for each template; OMIT customEvaluationMetricLabel; let the optimizer infer the grading label
explanation: Advanced Prompt Optimization requires JSONL with ONE PROMPT TEMPLATE per line (not one sample per line, ruling out A), a FIXED version string (bedrock-2026-05-14, not a current date, ruling out B), DOUBLE-brace {{variableName}} placeholders (single braces in A don't match), and inputVariables keys matching those placeholders exactly. Mixing steeringCriteria with customLLMJConfig and omitting a required customEvaluationMetricLabel (D) are documented common mistakes. 6 templates/80 samples/3 models all fit within documented limits (10 templates, 100 samples, 5 models).
comparison_note: Direct continuation of batch-2's 057 — same Advanced Prompt Optimization JSONL schema, applied to a different domain (outage notifications vs the earlier scenario) with the SAME fixed-version-string and double-brace-placeholder traps.

question: A pharma quality team has separate MCP servers for batch-record lookup, lab-instrument status, and change-control ticket search. The MCP client must connect to ONE endpoint and discover a MERGED tool catalog before invoking tools — no rewriting existing MCP servers, no new hosted containers. Best implementation?
options: A) Configure AgentCore Gateway with each MCP server as an MCP TARGET; connect the client to the Gateway endpoint
B) Configure AgentCore Gateway with each MCP server as a RUNTIME target; route requests by path from the Gateway endpoint
C) Create Lambda targets in AgentCore Gateway as ADAPTER TOOLS that call the existing MCP servers; maintain ToolDefinitions for each exposed tool
D) Configure AgentCore Gateway with each MCP server as an HTTP target; route tool calls directly through the Gateway endpoint
explanation: AgentCore Gateway's MCP TARGET type is documented specifically for connecting PRE-EXISTING MCP servers with aggregation mode — the gateway acts as one virtual MCP server presenting a consolidated tools/list. HTTP targets (D) and Runtime targets (B) forward traffic/requests WITHOUT aggregation or protocol translation. Lambda targets (C) require building adapter code and maintaining ToolDefinitions manually — unnecessary when MCP targets natively aggregate existing MCP servers with zero rewriting.
comparison_note: Fills in the AgentCore Gateway target-type taxonomy referenced as distractors in batch-2's 060 (which chose ECS/Fargate hosting for a single containerized MCP server) — this scenario is the case where Gateway MCP-target aggregation, not custom hosting, is the right answer because MULTIPLE pre-existing MCP servers need a single merged endpoint.

question: A mortgage-servicing assistant must: block unapproved debt-counseling topics, mask account numbers/taxpayer IDs, reject responses unsupported by retrieved servicing-policy excerpts, VERIFY fee/eligibility statements against an INTERNAL RULES API, and keep an auditable record of the approved FM's intended use/limitations. Enforcement before release, minimal custom policy code. Best design?
options: A) Bedrock guardrail w/ denied topics+sensitive-info filters+contextual grounding checks; maintain an approved MODEL CARD artifact; invoke a Lambda COMPLIANCE CHECK against the rules API before release
B) Bedrock Prompt Management w/ a policy-only template+few-shot examples; maintain prompt version history; run a Lambda SAMPLING JOB AFTER messages are stored
C) Lambda pre/post-processing w/ Comprehend entity detection; maintain a model card artifact; DISABLE managed guardrails to centralize all checks in code
D) Bedrock guardrail w/ denied topics+sensitive-info filters (no grounding); maintain a model card artifact; RELY ON FM PROMPT INSTRUCTIONS to validate fees/eligibility
explanation: Guardrails' contextual grounding checks directly address 'unsupported by retrieved excerpts,' while fee/eligibility rules are DETERMINISTIC BUSINESS LOGIC requiring a Lambda call to the internal rules API — neither prompt instructions (D) nor few-shot examples (B) provide a reliable deterministic compliance mechanism. A model card DOCUMENTS governance (intended use/limitations) but doesn't perform runtime enforcement. Disabling managed guardrails to centralize everything in custom code (C) increases operational burden and drops the managed grounding capability.
group: Guardrails + Deterministic Business-Rule Gate (Model Card + Rules API)
comparison_note: Same guardrails-plus-deterministic-Lambda-gate pattern as batch-2's 044 (Automated Reasoning checks for coverage rules) — this scenario uses a plain rules-API call rather than Automated Reasoning checks, since the fee/eligibility rules aren't necessarily expressed as formal logic policies.
