question: An FM release policy requires an UNATTENDED CI/CD regression gate against two fixed S3 JSONL benchmarks (summarization, classification), each 950 prompts with ground truth, PLUS a separate QUARTERLY HUMAN PREFERENCE REVIEW comparing current vs candidate model outputs. All results archived in S3; pipeline must NOT promote merely because a job was submitted. (Select TWO.)
options: A) Create AUTOMATED model evaluation jobs SEPARATELY for each model version and task type; write results to S3; block promotion until each job reaches Completed and passes thresholds
B) Create a HUMAN-WORKER model evaluation job with the current and candidate model inference configurations; collect worker ratings/preferences; store review output in S3
C) Create an LLM-AS-A-JUDGE evaluation with a generator+judge model; collect evaluator explanations; use those scores AS the quarterly human preference review
D) Create ONE automated model evaluation job that includes BOTH model versions AND BOTH task types; write results to S3; compare metrics when CreateEvaluationJob returns a jobArn
E) Create CloudWatch alarms on AWS/Bedrock invocation latency/token counts/throttles/errors; promote releases when runtime metrics stay within baseline ranges
explanation: Automated jobs support ONE model/inference profile and ONE task type per job, requiring SEPARATE jobs (A) — combining both models AND both task types into one job (D) violates both limits, and a returned jobArn only means ACCEPTED, not completed. Human-worker jobs specifically support TWO-model comparison (B), directly satisfying the quarterly human-preference requirement — LLM-as-a-judge (C) uses an EVALUATOR MODEL, not human workers, so it can't substitute for the human review. Runtime CloudWatch metrics (E) are operational signals, not semantic quality gates.
group: Human-Based vs Automatic Model Evaluation (Multi-Model Comparison)
comparison_note: Same human-based-two-model-comparison-vs-automated-one-model-limit distinction as this batch's 112 — 112 focuses on the CORS infrastructure requirement for human-eval jobs, this one focuses on combining automated PER-TASK-TYPE regression gates with the SEPARATE human-preference review in one release policy.

question: An aerospace RAG assistant spans six certification domains, each independently reindexed. Approved OpenSearch Service managed clusters are public-access, governed by approved policies (the only permitted customer-managed vector store). Must use Bedrock Knowledge Bases retrieval+citations, not a custom retrieval service. Best architecture?
options: A) One customer-managed KB per domain, each backed by a separate OpenSearch index using the FAISS engine, w/ LARGER vector dimensions to fit FUTURE embedding model upgrades
B) One customer-managed KB per domain, each backed by a separate FAISS-engine OpenSearch index, configuring ONLY THE VECTOR FIELD mapping with the embedding model dimensions
C) One customer-managed KB per domain, each backed by a separate OpenSearch index using the NMSLIB engine, configuring vector+text-chunk+metadata field mappings with the embedding model dimensions
D) One customer-managed KB per domain, each backed by a separate FAISS-engine OpenSearch index, configuring VECTOR, TEXT CHUNK, AND METADATA field mappings with the embedding model dimensions
explanation: FAISS (not NMSLIB, ruling out C) is required for this OpenSearch Service Bedrock KB setup. Vector dimensions must match the CURRENT embedding model — overprovisioning for a hypothetical future model (A) creates an incompatible mapping today. Bedrock KB needs mappings for ALL THREE roles — vector field, text chunk field, AND metadata field (B configures only the vector field, leaving Bedrock unable to associate chunks/metadata during retrieval).
comparison_note: Fourth entry in the recurring OpenSearch-faiss-engine-requirement family (batch-2's 012/019/024, batch-1's implicit references) — this scenario adds the complete-field-mapping trap (vector+text+metadata all required) and the current-vs-future-dimensions trap on top of the faiss/nmslib distinction.

question: A medical device manufacturer's OpenSearch domain (SEARCH account) needs semantic search where embedding generation happens THROUGH the search ingestion/query workflows (not a separate app worker), using an approved Bedrock embedding model whose invocation is controlled by a SEPARATE AI SERVICES account. Vector index must stay in the search account. (Select TWO.)
options: A) Configure OpenSearch neural search to use a REMOTE INFERENCE CONNECTOR that invokes the approved Bedrock embedding model during indexing and querying
B) Configure Bedrock Knowledge Bases in the AI SERVICES account to use the EXISTING OpenSearch vector index and manage embedding during sync/retrieval
C) Create the connector execution role DIRECTLY IN THE AI SERVICES ACCOUNT, grant it Bedrock invocation permissions, configure the search account's OpenSearch domain to use that role ARN
D) Configure OpenSearch neural search to register an OPENSEARCH-HOSTED embedding model on the existing domain and use it in ingestion/query pipelines

E) Create a connector execution role IN THE SEARCH ACCOUNT that OpenSearch Service can assume; grant the connector creator iam:PassRole for that role; allow the role to ASSUME a Bedrock invocation role in the AI services account
explanation: OpenSearch neural search's remote inference connector keeps embedding generation INSIDE the OpenSearch ingestion/query flow (A) — Bedrock Knowledge Bases (B) would shift the control plane to Bedrock, which the requirement rules out. The precise IAM detail: OpenSearch Service ASSUMES the connector execution role, so that role must live IN THE SEARCH (domain's) ACCOUNT (E) — not directly in the AI services account (C is backwards). The connector creator needs iam:PassRole for the role, and the role then assumes a Bedrock-invocation role cross-account. An OpenSearch-hosted embedding model (D) doesn't use the APPROVED Bedrock model governed by the AI services account.

question: A managed civil-engineering building-code KB has filterable jurisdiction+edition metadata. App retrieves excerpts THEN sends chunks to a SEPARATE model call with a custom prompt. Queries mix exact section IDs with natural language. Current code requests 40 chunks EVERY query and does custom Lambda reranking, increasing latency and sometimes including irrelevant cross-jurisdiction excerpts. Best fix preserving the existing generation flow?
options: A) Call RetrieveAndGenerate w/ managedSearchConfiguration, set numberOfResults closer to the displayed count, andAll filter jurisdiction+edition, reuse its citations
B) Call Retrieve w/ managedSearchConfiguration, set numberOfResults closer to the displayed excerpt count, andAll filter for jurisdiction AND edition, REMOVE Lambda reranking
C) Call Retrieve w/ vectorSearchConfiguration, overrideSearchType=HYBRID, andAll filter, remove Lambda reranking
D) Call Retrieve w/ managedSearchConfiguration, numberOfResults reduced, orAll filter for jurisdiction+edition, remove Lambda reranking
explanation: The app already has a SEPARATE generation step with a custom prompt — RetrieveAndGenerate (A) would add unwanted generation, changing the flow. Managed KBs use managedSearchConfiguration (not vectorSearchConfiguration, ruling out C) with hybrid search and DEFAULT managed reranking already built in, so removing the custom Lambda reranker and just reducing numberOfResults plus an andAll filter (needing BOTH jurisdiction AND edition to match) directly narrows the candidate set. orAll (D) is LESS selective — it can match right-edition-wrong-jurisdiction or vice versa, reintroducing exactly the cross-jurisdiction relevance problem.
group: Managed KB Retrieve Filter & numberOfResults Tuning
comparison_note: Sixth entry in the managed-KB-retrieval family (batch-2's 083/103/104/111/028/029/036, this batch's 124) — this one is specifically about the andAll-vs-orAll filter-logic trap plus reducing numberOfResults instead of custom reranking.

question: An auto-insurance RAG app runs OUTSIDE Bedrock (proprietary retriever). Must evaluate retrieval quality INDEPENDENTLY from generated-answer quality, avoid re-invoking the generator for STORED response records, include safety checks (harmful/biased wording), and get licensed-adjuster usefulness ratings. Evaluation automation creates jobs via API calls (valid metric names required). Dataset: 1,350 JSONL records in S3 — 700 single-turn retrieval probes w/ reference contexts, 650 response records w/ conversations up to 5 turns. LEAST custom evaluation code?
options: A) Split into retrieval+response datasets BELOW the job limit; RETRIEVE-ONLY RAG eval for the external retriever; RETRIEVE-AND-GENERATE RAG eval w/ BRING-YOUR-OWN inference response data; human-worker eval for adjuster ratings
B) Split into single-turn+conversation datasets below job limit; RETRIEVE-ONLY RAG evals for BOTH; select context relevance+coverage metrics; route low-scoring cases to human-worker eval
C) Split below job limit; LLM-as-a-judge model evaluations over stored responses+contexts; select correctness/faithfulness/helpfulness/harmfulness metrics; add human-worker eval for adjuster ratings

D) Submit the FULL 1,350-record dataset to ONE retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job; select context coverage+citation precision+faithfulness+harmfulness; add human-worker eval from the same job results
explanation: Retrieve-only RAG evaluation supports ONLY single-turn prompts — it can't evaluate the 650 multi-turn (up to 5-turn) stored response records (ruling out B). A single job supports up to 1,000 prompts, so 1,350 records in ONE job (D) exceeds the limit, and 'citation precision' isn't a valid documented metric name for the API. Retrieve-and-generate evaluation supports BRING-YOUR-OWN inference response data — letting the team evaluate the ALREADY-STORED generated responses WITHOUT re-invoking the generator model. LLM-as-a-judge (C) evaluates generated responses well but doesn't use the managed retrieve-only path for independently assessing the PROPRIETARY retriever's context relevance/coverage.
group: RAG Evaluation: External Retriever + Bring-Your-Own Response Data
comparison_note: Extends the evaluation-jobs family (batch-2's 013/023/029/040/043/060(this batch)) with the BRING-YOUR-OWN-response-data feature specifically — the key differentiator letting an external, non-Bedrock retriever/generator pipeline still use managed Bedrock RAG evaluation without redundant re-generation.

question: Reviewers must correlate a generated evidence-summary SENTENCE (months later) back to its cataloged source location, schema/source properties, original document attribution, AND the user invocation that produced it. Source inventory: scanned manuals + eligibility exports cataloged by Glue crawlers and manual definitions. Minimize custom provenance code, avoid relying on displayed footnotes as the ONLY audit artifact. Best implementation?
options: A) Register sources in Glue Data Catalog, attach document-level source attributes during KB ingestion, invoke RetrieveAndGenerate, STORE generatedResponsePart AND retrievedReferences from citations WITH CloudTrail audit records
B) Register in Glue, attach attributes, invoke RetrieveAndGenerate, store MODEL INVOCATION LOGS and FINAL ANSWER TEXT with CloudTrail
C) Register in Glue, attach attributes, invoke RETRIEVE (not RetrieveAndGenerate), store the retrieved chunk array with a CUSTOM sentence-to-source mapper and CloudTrail
D) Register in Glue, attach FILE URI attributes, invoke RetrieveAndGenerate, store ONLY knowledge base source LOCATIONS with CloudTrail
explanation: RetrieveAndGenerate's Citation objects (generatedResponsePart + retrievedReferences) give the STRUCTURED, MACHINE-READABLE generated-sentence-to-source mapping — persisting those (not just model logs/final text in B, and not just source URIs in D) preserves the deterministic audit trail. Glue Data Catalog supplies the registered technical metadata (location, schema, properties) that citations alone don't carry. Using Retrieve alone (C) requires building a custom mapper — exactly the provenance code the requirement wants minimized.
group: Provenance via Glue Data Catalog + RetrieveAndGenerate Citations
comparison_note: Same Citation-object-plus-Glue-Data-Catalog provenance pattern as batch-1's Q25 — nearly identical scenario reapplied here, reinforcing that generatedResponsePart+retrievedReferences (not invocation logs, not bare source URIs) is the documented audit-trail mechanism.

question: A staffing platform uses a SageMaker endpoint (scoring) and a Bedrock FM (screening explanations). New regulations require CONTINUOUS fairness monitoring across protected demographic groups, NEAR-REAL-TIME blocking of policy-violating explanations, automated escalation, and audit records WITHOUT raw PII. (Select TWO.)
options: A) CloudTrail Lake as the PRIMARY evidence store for Bedrock invocations; analyze logged events for prompt/response violations
B) Enable SageMaker Model Monitor DATA QUALITY checks for the endpoint; alarm on schema drift; use alerts as fairness evidence
C) Write encrypted app audit logs to an S3 evidence bucket; apply lifecycle retention; use Macie findings for LATER remediation
D) Configure SAGEMAKER CLARIFY bias monitoring for the scoring endpoint; publish results to CloudWatch; trigger remediation workflows from alarms
E) Apply BEDROCK GUARDRAILS to generated explanations; REDACT prompt/response artifacts BEFORE audit logging; route violations to reviewers
explanation: SageMaker Clarify (D) is the bias-SPECIFIC monitoring integration with Model Monitor — generic data-quality/schema-drift checks (B) don't measure demographic-group fairness. For the Bedrock generation path, Guardrails enforce policy in near-real-time, but the audit requirement ('no raw PII') demands REDACTING artifacts BEFORE storage (E) — encrypting/retaining then discovering sensitive data LATER via Macie (C) still retains unredacted content first. CloudTrail (A) records API activity, not full model interaction evidence.
group: Fairness/Bias Monitoring: SageMaker Clarify + Bedrock Guardrails
comparison_note: Same two-separate-risk-controls principle as batch-2's 066 (encrypted logs vs guardrails, redact-then-store vs discover-then-remediate) — 066 is the general framework question, this one adds the SPECIFIC pairing of SageMaker Clarify (for the scoring endpoint) with Bedrock Guardrails (for the generation path).

question: A recipe assistant must classify requests by complexity, route simple substitutions to a SMALL low-cost FM, route multi-course planning to a LARGER FM, and run allergen-sensitive responses through TWO DIFFERENT FMs before a deterministic policy check chooses the final JSON. PMs need to adjust routing conditions and prompt steps WITHOUT redeploying; developers can maintain a small amount of aggregation code. Best implementation?
options: A) Bedrock Agent w/ action groups invoking separate Lambda functions for each model selection/aggregation step
B) Step Functions state machine w/ Lambda tasks invoking each model, ALL routing logic implemented IN CODE
C) Bedrock Flow w/ conditional branches to specialized prompt nodes, invoke a Lambda node for DETERMINISTIC aggregation
D) Bedrock prompt router that sends each request to a lower-cost or higher-capability model and returns the selected model's output
explanation: Bedrock Flows lets PMs adjust conditional branches and prompt steps as a managed workflow WITHOUT redeployment, while keeping only the deterministic policy-check/aggregation logic in a small Lambda node — a full Step Functions+Lambda build (B) pushes ALL routing logic into code, defeating the no-redeploy requirement. A Bedrock Agent (A) is built for the MODEL to dynamically choose tools, not for PM-adjustable explicit branching. Bedrock's intelligent prompt router (D) optimizes cost/capability selection but isn't a multi-step workflow supporting parallel dual-FM review plus custom aggregation.
group: Bedrock Flows for Multi-Path Model Routing

question: A pharma clinical-documentation team has TWO features (discharge-summary drafting, patient-question answering), each with 900 representative prompts in valid .jsonl datasets. Wants a FULLY AUTOMATED first-pass evaluation preserving task-specific metrics, evaluating TWO inference profiles, using ALL 1,800 prompts if the managed service supports it, no custom evaluator. Best plan?
options: A) TWO automatic jobs (one per inference profile); COMBINE both feature datasets into ONE .jsonl file; select BOTH task types; configure IAM role+S3 output
B) TWO automatic jobs (one per task type); configure BOTH inference profiles IN EACH JOB; use the matching .jsonl dataset; configure IAM role+S3 output
C) FOUR automatic jobs (one per profile+task type); use the BUILT-IN prompt dataset for each task type; configure IAM role+S3 output
D) FOUR automatic jobs (one per inference profile and task type); use the MATCHING .jsonl dataset for each job; configure IAM role+S3 output
explanation: Automatic evaluation jobs enforce BOTH constraints simultaneously — one TASK TYPE per job (ruling out A's combined-both-task-types approach) AND one MODEL/inference profile per job (ruling out B's both-profiles-in-one-job approach) — so 2 profiles × 2 task types requires exactly FOUR separate jobs. Built-in prompt datasets (C) are randomly downsampled to 100 prompts, discarding the team's full 900-prompt representative sets — each job must use its MATCHING custom .jsonl dataset (each within the documented 1,000-prompt limit).
group: Automatic Evaluation Job Matrix (Multi-Profile x Multi-Task-Type)
comparison_note: Same job-count-equals-profiles-times-task-types matrix logic as this batch's 068 (identical scenario structure, reused here to reinforce the rule) — both scenarios land on exactly FOUR jobs from a 2×2 profile/task-type combination.

question: An artifact-cataloging Lambda reads a JPEG + curator note, invokes Claude 3 Sonnet via DIRECT InvokeModel. No separate OCR/captioning service; must keep direct runtime calls; must provide BOTH image and note in the SAME inference request. Current body puts image bytes and note in SEPARATE TOP-LEVEL fields — validation fails. What change?
options: A) JSON body w/ model params, a TOP-LEVEL prompt string, and inline base64 image data in a separate field
B) JSON body w/ model params, a USER MESSAGE, and CONTENT BLOCKS for the instruction text AND base64-encoded image data
C) JSON body w/ model params, a user message, and an S3 OBJECT URI for the image inside the instruction text
D) JSON body w/ model params, a user message, and a VECTOR EMBEDDING generated from the image bytes
explanation: Claude 3 multimodal InvokeModel calls use the provider's messages-style structure with TYPED CONTENT BLOCKS (text and image) inside a user message — arbitrary top-level fields for image bytes (A) don't match this schema. An S3 URI in the prompt text (C) is treated as plain text; the model never fetches it. A vector embedding (D) discards visual detail and isn't the multimodal input format Claude expects.
group: Direct InvokeModel Multimodal Schema (Claude Messages API)
comparison_note: Continues the direct-InvokeModel-schema thread from this batch's 082 (Titan Image Generator) and batch-2's 050 (Titan Embeddings/Claude text Messages API) — same 'InvokeModel body is model-specific, never universal' principle, now applied to Claude's MULTIMODAL (image+text) content-block structure.

question: A game-studio player-support chat assistant (public REST API → Lambda → Bedrock) sees messages with emails/phones/account IDs/session tokens. Must reduce sensitive values reaching the model, enforce safety on BOTH user messages and generated replies, return ONLY JSON matching the mobile contract. Layered protections, minimal custom ML development. Best implementation?
options: A) API GW request validation; add prohibited-content rules to the SYSTEM PROMPT; call Bedrock from Lambda; RETRY GENERATION until the response passes Lambda JSON validation
B) API GW request validation; Lambda preprocessor applies Comprehend+pattern matching; call Bedrock WITH GUARDRAILS; validate AND REDACT the response in Lambda before returning JSON
C) API GW request validation; Lambda preprocessor applies Comprehend+pattern matching; call Bedrock WITHOUT guardrails; validate the response SCHEMA in Lambda
D) API GW request validation; call Bedrock WITH guardrails from Lambda; invoke Comprehend on the GENERATED RESPONSE ONLY; redact unsafe fields before returning JSON
explanation: Defense-in-depth needs controls BEFORE (Comprehend+pattern matching reduces sensitive values pre-invocation), DURING (Bedrock guardrails enforce safety policy on both input and output), and AFTER (Lambda validates/redacts the final JSON contract) — prompt-instruction-plus-retry (A) is an anti-pattern relying on probabilistic compliance, skipping guardrails (C) drops the managed safety layer, and output-only PII handling (D) fails the explicit 'reduce sensitive values that reach the model' requirement.
group: Layered PII + Guardrail Defense (Pre- and Post-Inference)
comparison_note: Same three-layer (pre/during/post) defense pattern as batch-2's 070/075/099/036 — reinforces that PII reduction must happen BEFORE model invocation, not only as output filtering, across yet another scenario variant.

question: An IRB classification-decision workflow must stop before publishing whenever human review is required (up to 30 DAYS). The reviewer portal runs in a SHARED SERVICES account; the Step Functions workflow and publishing resources run in a SEPARATE WORKLOAD account. Review wait must stay part of a durable auditable execution, avoid idle compute. Best implementation?
options: A) Standard workflow, Lambda callback task sends an approval link w/ $$.Task.Token for an API GW endpoint IN THE WORKLOAD ACCOUNT, a WORKLOAD-ACCOUNT Lambda calls SendTaskSuccess/Failure after submission
B) EXPRESS workflow writes a pending approval record to DynamoDB and ENDS; an API GW endpoint updates the record and starts a publishing workflow after submission
C) Standard workflow, Lambda callback task sends $$.Task.Token to the SHARED SERVICES PORTAL, the PORTAL'S SHARED-SERVICES-ACCOUNT Lambda calls SendTaskSuccess/Failure
D) Standard workflow writes a pending approval record to DynamoDB, enters WAIT STATES, invokes Lambda PERIODICALLY to check the reviewer portal, publishes when a decision is found
explanation: Task tokens MUST be returned by a principal in the SAME AWS ACCOUNT as the workflow — since the workflow runs in the workload account, the callback endpoint/Lambda must ALSO be there (A), not the shared services account where the portal happens to run (C is a cross-account violation, even though the portal is 'closer' organizationally). Express workflows (B) can't sustain a single durable 30-day execution. Wait-state polling (D) adds unneeded delay versus direct callback resumption.
comparison_note: Third occurrence of this EXACT pattern (batch-2's 021, 096) — same same-account task-token rule and Standard-vs-Express duration limit, now with the added twist that the 'natural' organizational choice (routing through the shared-services portal's own account) is the wrong answer.

question: ECS tasks in private subnets must invoke Bedrock WITHOUT internet access. Security requires BOTH IAM and endpoint-policy restrictions to approved roles/model ARNs. Invocation logging must handle payloads >100KB and BINARY output, logs must stay same-account/Region. Which design meets these requirements?
options: A) A `bedrock` CONTROL-PLANE VPC endpoint, an endpoint policy, and CloudWatch Logs as the ONLY invocation-log destination
B) A `bedrock-runtime` VPC endpoint w/ a restrictive endpoint policy AND IAM policies, but send invocation logs ONLY to CloudWatch Logs
C) A `bedrock-runtime` VPC endpoint w/ PRIVATE DNS, RESTRICTIVE endpoint AND IAM policies, and model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs PLUS an S3 destination in the same account/Region
D) A `bedrock-runtime` VPC endpoint w/ its DEFAULT policy, relying ONLY on IAM identity policies
explanation: Inference calls use the `bedrock-runtime` endpoint (not the control-plane `bedrock` endpoint, ruling out A). A VPC endpoint alone isn't an authorization boundary — the DEFAULT endpoint policy allows full Bedrock access through it (ruling out D), so a RESTRICTIVE custom endpoint policy plus scoped IAM policies together provide the required defense-in-depth. CloudWatch Logs alone caps inline JSON at 100KB and can't hold binary data — S3 delivery in the same account/Region is required alongside it (ruling out B).
group: Private VPC Access to bedrock-runtime + S3 Logging
comparison_note: Same bedrock-runtime-plus-restrictive-endpoint-policy-plus-S3-for-large/binary-payloads pattern as batch-2's 049 (which added the Lake Formation governance layer) — this scenario strips that down to the pure networking/logging requirements without the data-lake permission complexity.

question: A maritime insurance RAG assistant answers coverage questions; adjusters often ask the SAME business question with DIFFERENT wording, and the corpus gets a new VERSION IDENTIFIER whenever policies change. Must reduce expensive generation calls and improve p95, but cached answers can be reused ONLY when the prior request is a HIGH-CONFIDENCE MATCH for the current question AND the SAME corpus version. Best caching design?
options: A) Deterministic hash of each normalized question; store answers in DynamoDB w/ TTL scoped by corpus version; invoke Bedrock on hash misses
B) Configure CloudFront to cache responses by normalized query string+corpus version, short TTLs, forward misses to API Gateway
C) Enable Bedrock PROMPT CACHING for static instructions/boilerplate, reuse cached prompt PREFIXES, invoke Bedrock for EVERY adjusted question
D) Generate an EMBEDDING for each normalized question, search a MemoryDB VECTOR INDEX for a thresholded cache hit scoped by corpus version, invoke Bedrock on misses
explanation: Exact-match approaches (hash-based DynamoDB in A, CloudFront query-string caching in B) can't recognize PARAPHRASED questions with the same intent — only embedding-based similarity search (D) with a confidence THRESHOLD, scoped by corpus version, achieves that. Bedrock prompt caching (C) reduces repeated PROMPT PROCESSING cost/latency for a static prefix, but the model is STILL INVOKED every time — it doesn't reuse completed answers, missing the core 'avoid generation calls' goal.
group: Semantic/Vector Response Caching vs Prompt Caching
comparison_note: Distinct new lever in the token/cost-optimization space (batch-2's 011/018/032) — this scenario is specifically about SEMANTIC RESPONSE reuse (avoiding generation entirely) rather than input pruning, output capping, or model routing.

question: A claims-summary app uses a PROVISIONED THROUGHPUT ARN for baseline daily traffic. During hurricanes, unpredictable spikes exceed committed capacity. Must keep using EXISTING committed capacity for normal traffic, must NOT buy additional committed capacity for rare events, is approved for ANY supported commercial Region. The FM has a Global Cross-Region inference profile; team wants the BROADEST documented regional pool. Best solution?
options: A) Keep the provisioned throughput ARN for baseline; route overflow to DIRECT ON-DEMAND model identifiers in selected commercial Regions
B) Keep the provisioned throughput ARN for baseline; route overflow invocations to the GLOBAL Cross-Region inference profile by setting the profile as the model identifier
C) Keep the provisioned throughput ARN for baseline; RETRY overflow invocations against the SAME ARN with exponential backoff and jitter
D) Keep the provisioned throughput ARN for baseline; route overflow to a GEOGRAPHIC Cross-Region inference profile for the source geography
explanation: Cross-Region Inference is invoked by passing an inference profile as modelId — GLOBAL profiles route to ANY supported commercial Region worldwide (matching 'broadest pool'), while GEOGRAPHIC profiles (D) are narrower (bounded to one geography). Inference profiles currently do NOT support Provisioned Throughput, so this must be a SPLIT design: keep the provisioned ARN for predictable baseline, add the Global profile ONLY for overflow (B) — bypassing the managed profile with direct on-demand regional calls (A) recreates custom failover logic Bedrock's managed routing already provides; retrying against the SAME saturated ARN (C) adds no new capacity.
group: Cross-Region Inference Profile for Burst Overflow (Global vs Geographic)
comparison_note: Fifth entry in the Global-vs-Geographic-Cross-Region-profile family (batch-2's 062/098, this batch's 081/119/123) — this scenario's unique framing is PAIRING Provisioned Throughput (baseline) WITH a Cross-Region profile (overflow only), since profiles can't replace committed capacity outright.

question: A water-utility incident-report assistant routes free text to different FMs (customer notices, regulatory explanations, engineering troubleshooting, multilingual summaries) based on SEMANTIC INTENT and a confidence score from a lightweight classifier. Low-confidence requests use a GENERAL-PURPOSE model. Ops must adjust confidence thresholds DURING STORM EVENTS without changing clients, plus retry handling and route-level observability. Best implementation?
options: A) Lambda router w/ ENVIRONMENT-VARIABLE thresholds, applies KEYWORD RULES to the prompt, calls the selected Bedrock model, writes route metrics to CloudWatch
B) Step Functions workflow runs a Lambda routing task, reads thresholds from AWS APPCONFIG, classifies the prompt, branches to the selected Bedrock invocation, logs the route decision
C) Step Functions workflow invokes ALL candidate Bedrock models IN PARALLEL, compares responses in a Lambda aggregation task, returns the response with the highest score
D) API Gateway request validators+mapping templates normalize fields, enforce schema, pass an EXPLICIT ROUTE HINT to one Lambda integration, Lambda invokes Bedrock
explanation: AppConfig externalizes thresholds so ops can adjust them at RUNTIME during storms WITHOUT redeploying or changing clients — environment variables (A) require a function configuration update for every change. Step Functions gives the retry/catch behavior and execution history for route-level observability that a plain Lambda router lacks. Keyword rules (A) are a weak substitute for genuine semantic classification; an explicit route hint from the client (D) skips classification-based routing entirely; invoking ALL candidate models in parallel (C) is a cost/latency anti-pattern when the goal is selecting the BEST model before inference, not ensemble voting.
group: Semantic Model Routing with Step Functions + AppConfig
comparison_note: Same AppConfig-driven-routing-without-redeployment principle as batch-2's 086 (model/tenant/task routing via AppConfig Lambda extension) and the model-cascade group (batch-2's 057/011) — this scenario combines semantic CLASSIFICATION-based routing with Step Functions orchestration rather than a static configuration lookup.
